Article Title: Iconic 1880s Rhode Island waterfront social club is being offered for the first time in 50 years; after a $1.2 million price cut, the historic five-bedroom property now asks $9.75 million
Article Text:

Pic credit: Sotheby's Realty

Back in the day, it was a men's club with a bed and breakfast

Pic credit: Sotheby's Realty

Pic credit: Sotheby's Realty

The Reading Room, one of Narragansett's most iconic properties, has hit the market for the first time in over 50 years. The five-bedroom house is for sale for $9.75 million after a price cut. It was first listed in June at $10.95 million, Realtor.com reported. Built in 1880 as a social club, the property stands beside The Towers and is the last surviving remnant of the grand Narragansett Pier Casino.The house began in the late 1800s as a liquor-free men's club. “It was originally a social club in the 1880s and was a reading room where men would gather to smoke cigars,” listing agent John Hodnett of Hopewell Real Estate told the outlet. Historian Winifred J.W. Kissouth described it as a liquor-free men's bed-and-breakfast club where members went to read and smoke, according to The Boston Globe. Some of its famous visitors included Jerome Bonaparte, a relative of Napoleon Bonaparte, and New York surgeon Dr Charles Hitchcock.The building did not stay where it was originally built. The Reading Room was moved from Mathewson Street to its present location on Ocean Road in the late 1890s, according to documentation from the National Register of Historic Places.The move made it part of the Narragansett Pier Casino. At the time, ‘casino’ often referred to social clubs rather than gambling halls, which surprises many visitors today.“It was relocated to its current location to be a part of the casino. Now, it’s ideally located minutes away from the town beach, cafes and restaurants,” Hodnett added.The neighbouring building is The Towers, the only surviving remnant of the casino after a series of fires, nor'easters and hurricanes. From the house, you can see both the bay and the landmark, and the view is a big reason people remember the property.In 2010, the house underwent a major restoration that brought back its Victorian character. The project received historic-preservation recognition from Preserve Rhode Island and the Rhody Awards. Many of its original features survived, including the hardwood floors, bay windows, grand staircase, stained glass, high ceilings, period chandeliers and three fireplaces.“This property enjoys sweeping water-view porches, water views from almost every room, intricate details, multiple year-round sun porches, historic chandeliers and a unique Tower Room,” the listing on Sotheby's Realty says. It describes the home as a “once-in-a-generation opportunity” to live in the heart of Narragansett.The house sits on 0.69 acres and spans 5,099 square feet, with five bedrooms, two full bathrooms and two half-bathrooms. Most historic homes on Narragansett Pier sit on smaller parcels, so this one offers something rare. Hodnett describes the setting as a village address with the feel of a private sanctuary. The property also includes a detached three-car garage, a covered front porch and multiple sunrooms, so the outdoor space is not limited to the lawn.The home could serve as the buyer's primary residence. According to the agent, much of the hard work has already been done. The restoration is complete, and a new owner can focus on shaping the interior to suit their lifestyle rather than repairing the structure.In June, the property was listed for $10.95 million. After sitting on the market for months, the price has fallen to $9.75 million. It is unclear why the price was reduced.
Article Summary: The Reading Room in Narragansett, Rhode Island, is for sale for $9.75 million. The five-bedroom house was built in 1880 as a liquor-free men's club. Some of its famous visitors included Jerome Bonaparte and Dr Charles Hitchcock. The house underwent a major restoration in 2010 that brought back its Victorian character. It is the last surviving remnant of the grand Narragsett Pier Casino.

Article Title: In 2022, a Nashville developer bought a vacant lot, but the city held its building permit for four years while weighing a future road; a federal appeals court has now revived its lawsuit over the free
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Why Nashville's development hold became a legal dispute

How the developer challenged the city's decision

What the Sixth Circuit decided

What the ruling could mean for property owners

A Nashville property developer has won a significant legal reprieve after a federal appeals court revived its lawsuit against the city over a building permit that remained on hold for four years. The dispute began in 2022, when SW Nashville EB Owner, LLC, bought a vacant parcel and sought permission to develop it, only for local authorities to suspend the application while considering a possible future road. According to the Pacific Legal Foundation, which represents the developer, the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit overturned a lower court's dismissal on August 14, 2026, allowing the legal challenge to proceed. The ruling raises broader questions about government planning powers and the constitutional protection of private property.SW Nashville purchased a four-acre property in Nashville's East Bank district in the spring of 2022. The company planned to remove a dilapidated building on the site and construct an apartment complex, according to the court record. It applied for standard construction permits, arguing that its proposed development complied with the applicable zoning requirements.However, Nashville's Metropolitan Government, commonly known as Metro, placed an indefinite hold on development applications affecting the property. The city was assessing possible routes for a major future roadway that could require part of the developer's land. The proposed road was still under consideration, but the permit freeze prevented the company from moving forward with its plans. The developer argued that it was left bearing the costs of ownership, including property taxes, maintenance and insurance, without being able to develop or sell the land.Pacific Legal Foundation stated that the restrictions had caused substantial financial losses. Its case page put the company's accumulated taxes and maintenance expenses at more than $8.2 million. The figure reflects the legal organisation's account of the developer's losses, rather than a final court finding on compensation.SW Nashville argued that keeping its property undevelopable for years, without formally rejecting the permit or acquiring the land, amounted to an unconstitutional taking. The company filed its lawsuit in May 2024, challenging the city's actions under the Takings and Due Process Clauses of the US Constitution, as well as the Takings Clause of the Tennessee Constitution. The case was subsequently transferred to federal court.The Fifth Amendment prohibits the government from taking private property for public use without just compensation. Although eminent domain allows authorities to acquire land for qualifying public projects, the Constitution requires compensation when a taking occurs. The developer's argument centred on whether a government can effectively prevent the use of private property indefinitely while deciding whether it might need that land for a future public project.The case was initially dismissed by the US District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. The lower court concluded that the developer's claims were premature because the city had not reached a final decision on the permit application, leaving the claims unripe for judicial review. SW Nashville appealed, arguing that the indefinite hold itself had already prevented development and caused measurable harm.In its August 14, 2026, decision in SW Nashville EB Owner, LLC v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County, the Sixth Circuit reversed the lower court's dismissal and sent the case back for further proceedings. The appeals court determined that the city's continuing development hold constituted a definitive decision for the purpose of deciding whether the developer's claims were ready for judicial review. The company did not have to wait indefinitely for a formal permit rejection when the existing restriction had already barred development.The court considered the practical effect of the city's actions, rather than treating the absence of a final written decision as sufficient reason to prevent the lawsuit from proceeding. Its ruling addressed the question of whether the claims were ripe for review, meaning whether the dispute had developed sufficiently for a court to consider it. Importantly, the appeals court did not finally establish that Nashville had violated the Constitution or order the city to pay compensation. Instead, it reversed the dismissal and remanded the case, allowing the lower court to continue considering the dispute and the remaining legal issues. The case will now return to the lower court, where unresolved issues, including statute-of-limitations arguments and qualified immunity, remain to be considered.The decision highlights a difficult balance between public infrastructure planning and private property rights. Cities need time to evaluate road networks, transport projects and other infrastructure requirements. However, prolonged restrictions can create serious financial consequences for owners whose land remains unusable while plans are being considered.The ruling does not prevent governments from planning future roads or acquiring land through lawful eminent-domain procedures. Rather, it indicates that an indefinite development freeze can be sufficiently definitive to allow a property owner's constitutional claims to be heard, even without a formal permit denial. The case could therefore matter to property owners facing similar restrictions, particularly where authorities prevent development while considering a possible future public project. Its ultimate impact will depend on how the lower court resolves the remaining issues.For SW Nashville, the immediate outcome is that its lawsuit can move forward after years of uncertainty. Whether the city must ultimately provide compensation, and whether the developer's constitutional claims succeed on their merits, remain unresolved.
Article Summary: SW Nashville EB Owner, LLC, bought a four-acre property in Nashville's East Bank district in the spring of 2022. The company planned to remove a dilapidated building on the site and construct an apartment complex. It applied for standard construction permits, arguing that its proposed development complied with the applicable zoning requirements. However, Nashville's Metropolitan Government, commonly known as Metro, placed an indefinite hold on development applications affecting the property. The city was assessing possible routes for a major future roadway that could require part of the land.

Article Title: Kentucky collected about 5,000 discarded Christmas trees in 2026 instead of sending them to landfills; officials sank 1,700 in a single lake to replace lost underwater shelter for fish
Article Text:
Natural materials can provide shelter for aquatic life (Kentucky Fish and Wildlife photo)

The problem beneath Kentucky's ageing lakes

How does it all begin?

Why Boltz Lake received 1,700 trees

How the project benefits people who fish

Thousands of Christmas trees that decorated homes during the holiday season have found a new purpose at the bottom of lakes in Kentucky. Around 5,000 trees were donated to a state-run recycling programme this year, with approximately 1,700 placed in Boltz Lake alone. The trees are being used to create underwater shelter for fish in lakes where natural hiding places have gradually disappeared.The effort is part of Christmas for the Fishes, a programme run by the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources. Now in its ninth season, the initiative collects used Christmas trees and places them underwater to help maintain habitats for different fish species.According to a FOX19, the trees were collected after the last holiday season and distributed among lakes selected for habitat restoration. Boltz Lake, located in Grant County, received a substantial share of the donations.But why would a lake need thousands of Christmas trees? Many of Kentucky's lakes are artificial, and the trees and other wooden structures that once provided shelter for fish have slowly broken down. Without these structures, fish have fewer places to hide, feed and reproduce.When a lake is created, submerged trees, logs and other natural materials can provide shelter for aquatic life.However, these structures do not last forever. As the wood decays, the spaces between branches and logs gradually disappear. This has become a concern in Kentucky, where many artificial lakes date back to the late 1950s and early 1960s.David Baker, a programme coordinator with Kentucky Fish and Wildlife, told FOX19 that the department has been working to replace the habitat lost over time.The solution involves something that is readily available after Christmas: discarded natural trees. Once submerged, their branches provide spaces where smaller fish can escape larger predators. They also offer shaded areas and places for fish to feed. In this way, trees that are no longer needed in homes can continue serving a useful purpose for several years.The process begins after Christmas, when residents bring their used trees to designated collection points. For the 2026 programme, Kentucky Fish and Wildlife accepted donations between December 26, 2025, and January 16, 2026. There were 37 collection locations across the state.However, not every type of Christmas decoration could be donated. The department accepted only real evergreen trees, with all lights, garlands and ornaments removed. Artificial trees and other plant materials were excluded.After collection, the trees were prepared for use in lakes and reservoirs. Rather than being scattered randomly, they were grouped together and secured using environmentally friendly weights.These groups of submerged trees create spaces between their branches. Small fish can move into these areas for protection, while larger fish may gather nearby to feed.Spencer Phillips, a fisheries biologist with Kentucky Fish and Wildlife, explained the importance of these structures in information published by the Jackson County Sun.“Every tree counts,” Phillips said. “Each tree can provide benefits for local fisheries for several years, gradually enhancing fish habitat that has been lost over time. Local anglers also benefit from the creation of reliable fishing hotspots around the sunken brush piles.”The department does not return to every lake annually. Instead, it follows a schedule under which individual lakes generally receive another round of trees every five to six years. This is because the submerged branches eventually deteriorate, just like the natural wooden structures they are intended to replace.During the latest season, approximately 1,700 of the 5,000 donated trees were placed in Boltz Lake. The remaining donations were part of the wider programme, which uses Christmas trees to improve fish habitats across Kentucky.By returning to different lakes over time, the department can continue replacing underwater shelter as older materials break down.The underwater trees are also useful to people who visit Kentucky's lakes for recreational fishing. Fish tend to gather around areas that offer shelter and food. As a result, locations where trees have been submerged can become places where anglers are more likely to find them. According to FOX19, crappie, bluegill and bass are among the fish commonly caught near these underwater structures.The department also makes it easier for anglers to locate the areas where trees have been placed. Officials record the GPS coordinates of the submerged structures and publish the information through the department's website and the FishBoatKY application. This means anglers can identify the locations of the artificial habitats before heading out onto the water.
Article Summary: Around 5,000 trees were donated to a state-run recycling programme. Approximately 1,700 of the trees were placed in Boltz Lake, Kentucky. The trees are being used to create underwater shelter for fish. Many of Kentucky's artificial lakes date back to the late 1950s and early 1960s.

Article Title: Rihanna launched Fenty Beauty in 2017 with a 40-shade foundation range; years later, its co-owner began exploring a sale of its 50% stake
Article Text:
Fenty Beauty entered the market with 40 foundation shades and a global launch

How the business grew beyond Rihanna's music career

How Rihanna and LVMH split ownership of Fenty Beauty

Rihanna's Fenty Beauty partnership faces a potential turning point

When Fenty Beauty arrived in 2017, one of its most talked-about features was something shoppers could see on the shelf: 40 foundation shades. For customers who had spent years mixing products or leaving a shop without finding a close match, the range addressed a familiar problem. Rihanna had entered the cosmetics business in partnership with LVMH, the luxury group behind some of the world's best-known fashion and beauty names. The launch soon grew into a business of its own, separate from the singer's recording career. The ownership arrangement that helped bring it to market would come back into focus years later, when LVMH began exploring a sale of its half-share.Fenty Beauty did not begin as a small local cosmetics line waiting to find an audience. Its September 2017 launch put the products in 1,600 stores across 17 countries. LVMH, Rihanna's business partner, brought experience in the luxury market, while the singer already had an international following. The scale of the release reflected both.The foundation collection drew particular attention. Forty shades gave shoppers a wider choice across fair, medium and deep complexions, including people who had often found the available options too limited.Other brands had worked on inclusive ranges before Fenty appeared, but the launch brought the issue into sharper public view. The phrase “Fenty effect” later came to describe the pressure on competitors to expand their own shade selections.Fenty Beauty found a commercial audience quickly. BBC reporting in 2021 put its sales at an estimated $100 million during the first 40 days after launch. Her connection to the products remained visible. Rihanna featured the brand on her social media accounts and spoke about its offerings, keeping Fenty in front of an audience that might otherwise have followed her mainly for music. The cosmetics business also gave her a source of wealth that did not depend on releasing albums or touring.Customers could buy Fenty through department stores and mainstream beauty retailers, including Boots in the UK. The products sat at a higher price point than some everyday make-up, but they were not confined to luxury department stores. That mix of positioning and availability helped the brand reach different groups of shoppers.By 2021, the scale of Rihanna's business interests was reflected in her estimated fortune. Forbes put her net worth at $1.7 billion, attributing about $1.4 billion to her interest in Fenty Beauty. Her other holdings included lingerie company Savage X Fenty, alongside earnings from music and acting. The figures showed just how much the cosmetics business had come to matter to her finances.Rihanna and LVMH each held a 50% stake in Fenty Beauty, according to Forbes' 2021 reporting. The arrangement gave the singer a direct interest in the company while linking the brand to a group with an established presence in luxury goods and cosmetics.It was a different proposition from simply licensing a celebrity's name to a make-up line. Rihanna remained closely identified with the products, while LVMH was the corporate partner behind the business. Their interests had been joined at the brand's launch, and the equal split meant that any later decision to sell one side's stake could change the ownership arrangement without necessarily ending Fenty Beauty itself.Years after the launch, LVMH began exploring a possible sale of its 50% holding. The move put the company's ownership under scrutiny, but exploring a transaction does not mean that a deal has been completed. A confirmed buyer, an agreed price and the final terms would be separate steps.For Rihanna, Fenty Beauty had become one of the most substantial parts of her business portfolio since its debut. The 40-shade foundation collection helped establish its identity, and its early international rollout gave it reach beyond the singer's existing audience. What happens to LVMH's stake would determine whether the original partnership continues in its current form. Until a sale is confirmed, however, the reported exploration remains a possible change in ownership, not a completed one.
Article Summary: Rihanna and LVMH each held a 50% stake in Fenty Beauty, according to Forbes' 2021 reporting. The arrangement gave the singer a direct interest in the company while linking the brand to a group with an established presence in luxury goods and cosmetics. By 2021, the scale of Rihanna's business interests was reflected in her estimated fortune.

Article Title: After 11 road accidents in four years, villagers in England spent four months knitting life-sized police officers and fake speed cameras; their handmade decoys are now making some drivers hit the brak
Article Text:
The appearance of the figures is unusual enough to make some motorists look twice (Representational photo)

Why villagers decided to make their own traffic officers

A four-month project attracts attention

Village's road safety plans

A group of villagers in England has spent four months making something they hope will persuade speeding motorists to slow down: life-sized knitted traffic officers and fake speed cameras. The unusual road safety campaign began after numerous accidents were recorded at a junction in Fillongley, Warwickshire, over four years. Since the handmade figures were installed last week, residents say they have noticed some drivers braking after mistaking them for real traffic enforcement equipment.According to BBC, members of the village's Knit and Natter group wanted to draw attention to a road safety problem that had troubled the community for years. That's when they decided to create figures that would be difficult for approaching motorists to ignore.Their work has appeared at several locations around Fillongley. Alongside the imitation traffic officers and speed cameras are knitted children carrying road safety messages and zebras placed above crossing signs. One figure, dressed in a Royal Air Force (RAF) uniform and a high-visibility vest, was also positioned beside the road holding a knitted speed gun.The campaign is particularly relevant to Nuneaton Road, where a busy crossroads has been a source of concern. Warwickshire County Council has recorded 11 traffic collisions at the junction over the past four years. A primary school is also located nearby. Residents say some drivers fail to pay attention to the speed limit signs, creating risks for people using the road.For residents, the knitted figures are more than an attempt to amuse passing motorists. They are a response to continuing concerns about road safety and the time being taken to introduce permanent improvements.Heather Badham, 58, a parish clerk and member of the knitting group, believes drivers approaching the junction from Nuneaton Road are responsible for many of the accidents.Speaking to Good News Network, she said, "90% of the accidents are caused by people coming down the Nuneaton road, not seeing the signs and then hitting someone."The village already has a flashing 30mph speed limit sign. However, Badham said some motorists continue to travel too fast despite the warning.By making figures resembling officers monitoring traffic, they hoped to make approaching drivers more conscious of their speed.Their efforts appear to have produced the reaction they wanted, at least among some motorists. Badham said residents had watched vehicles slow down as drivers noticed the roadside displays."Since putting these up, we have been chuckling as people saw the man and thought he was real. You could see the brake lights coming on," she said.These observations suggest the figures have caught drivers' attention, although there is no evidence yet that the campaign has reduced the number of accidents.The figures have become a talking point among people living in the village. Their appearance is unusual enough to make some motorists look twice, while the messages carried by other knitted characters explain why the displays have been placed there.Local resident Tom Docker, 42, was among those surprised by the work. "I certainly did a double take when I saw the one with the camera. I couldn’t believe it," he told Good News Network. He praised the effort behind the creations and said they were encouraging people to discuss the problem of speeding.But the attention has not been entirely positive. One of the group's most distinctive figures, the knitted RAF officer, has disappeared.According to the BBC, the character was made in memory of the father of one of the knitters, who had served in the RAF during the Second World War. It had been dressed in a knitted high-visibility vest and given a handmade speed gun.Badham said the figure had apparently been stolen during a short period in the morning. Its disappearance upset the group, particularly because of the work involved in making it. "This is a piece of village heritage, and it's just been taken by somebody," she told the BBC. The group is considering making a replacement and reporting the matter to police.The knitted campaign comes at a time when the future of the crossroads is already under discussion. Warwickshire County Council approved plans for traffic lights at the junction earlier this year. However, the proposal has not satisfied everyone. Some residents believe other measures, including average-speed cameras, should be considered.The council has said it is examining possible road safety improvements and waiting for confirmation from HS2 regarding funding for an alternative scheme.Warwickshire Police and Crime Commissioner Philip Seccombe has also recognised the seriousness of the problem, identifying Fillongley as one of the county's collision hotspots.
Article Summary: Villagers in Fillongley, Warwickshire, have spent four months making life-sized knitted traffic officers and fake speed cameras. The unusual road safety campaign began after numerous accidents were recorded at a junction over four years. Residents say some drivers fail to pay attention to the speed limit signs, creating risks for people using the road.

Article Title: US spent $861 million on agricultural pest inspections in 2011, but legal limits and fee collection failures left a $325 million funding gap
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Why did US agricultural inspection fees fall short of costs

Why did CBP receive only 60% of fees despite covering over 80% of costs

How did missed railcar fees cost the US $13.2 million in 2010

Why did US agricultural inspection fees remain insufficient

In 2011, the United States spent $861 million inspecting travellers and cargo for agricultural pests, but fees collected left a shortfall of more than $325 million. The funding gap stemmed partly from federal laws restricting which passengers and transport operators could be charged, alongside weaknesses in fee collection and differences between agency costs and revenue. According to the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the programme, jointly administered by the US Department of Agriculture and Customs and Border Protection, aims to intercept foreign agricultural pests and prevent prohibited materials from entering the country. Later reforms addressed some gaps, but legal restrictions remained.The GAO identified restrictions on the government’s fee-setting authority as one of the reasons for the shortfall. APHIS could not charge every person entering the United States, including pedestrians, under its authority. The agency was unable to recover the costs of those inspections by charging other parties. The report further identified commercial buses, private vessels and private aircraft as categories for which the existing legal framework restricted the collection of fees to cover passenger inspection costs.APHIS also chose not to charge certain passenger groups, citing difficulties associated with collecting small fees.These limitations meant that some inspection costs continued to be covered through federal appropriations rather than user fees. The GAO stated that additional legal authority would be necessary to recover all programme costs through fees. In its recommendations to Congress, the agency called for changes that would allow the Secretary of Agriculture to set rates covering the programme’s aggregate estimated costs and extend fee authority to additional transport categories.The report also identified a mismatch between the costs incurred by the two agencies and the revenue they received. In 2005, APHIS and CBP had agreed to distribute AQI fee collections in proportion to each agency’s share of programme costs. However, the GAO found that this arrangement was not reflected in the fiscal year 2011 figures. CBP incurred more than 80% of total programme costs but received only 60% of fee collections. APHIS, meanwhile, incurred 19% of costs and retained 36% of collections.CBP covered the difference between its AQI expenditure and its share of fee revenues through its annual appropriation. APHIS also carried forward part of its fee collections to maintain a shared reserve with CBP against unexpected declines in revenue. According to the GAO, APHIS aimed to maintain a reserve equivalent to three to five months of programme costs, but its preliminary fee proposal would have funded the reserve above the five-month maximum. The report warned that this level would increase reliance on appropriated funds to meet current programme costs.The GAO found that weaknesses in collection procedures also contributed to the funding problem. APHIS did not collect AQI fees for railcars in accordance with its regulations, resulting in a reported revenue loss of $13.2 million in 2010. CBP, meanwhile, did not verify that all fees due for commercial trucks, private aircraft and private vessels had been collected. The report said the resulting annual revenue loss for these categories was unknown.The report noted that CBP had tools available to address these collection problems but did not require their use. It recommended improvements to oversight and the allocation of inspection costs, including clearer guidance on recording officers’ work. The GAO also recommended that APHIS account for costs incurred by other federal agencies on behalf of the AQI programme when setting fees. These measures were intended to improve revenue collection and bring the distribution of fees closer to the actual costs of providing inspections.In October 2015, APHIS published a final rule introducing new AQI fee categories and adjusting existing rates. According to the GAO’s report update, the changes were intended to recover the full costs of related inspection services, including costs borne by other federal agencies. The changes included a $1.75 fee per cruise ship ticket for tickets purchased from 28 December 2015. The revised rules also removed caps on commercial cargo vessel and railcar fees and adjusted truck fees to better reflect inspection costs while retaining an incentive for trucks to use transponders.However, the changes did not eliminate every funding gap. The GAO’s update, dated February 2026, stated that Congress had not passed legislation giving the Secretary of Agriculture authority to set fees that fully recover the aggregate costs of AQI services. Rail passengers also continued to be exempt from AQI fees under the 2015 rule, leaving their inspection costs to be covered through CBP’s Salaries and Expenses appropriation. The GAO’s findings therefore identify both legal restrictions and administrative weaknesses as factors affecting the programme’s ability to fund agricultural inspections through fees.
Article Summary: In 2011, the United States spent $861 million inspecting travellers and cargo for agricultural pests, but fees collected left a shortfall of more than $325 million. The funding gap stemmed partly from federal laws restricting which passengers and transport operators could be charged, alongside weaknesses in fee collection.

Article Title: Russia’s digital Achilles’ heel? How Ukraine data centre strikes are disrupting daily life
Article Text:
Ukraine hits Russia’s tech nerve centre as data outages disrupt daily life (Representative Image)

Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centres have disrupted banking, taxi services, food deliveries and digital access to homes, exposing the vulnerability of services used by millions of Russians. This comes as Kyiv expands its campaign against Moscow’s technology infrastructure.The attacks, carried out over several days in October, targeted data centres operated by Yandex, Russia’s largest technology company, followed by a facility owned by Sberbank, the country’s largest bank. A data centre belonging to technology group VK was also reportedly targeted.Yandex, often described as “Russia’s Google”, provides search, email, navigation, music, ride-hailing, food delivery, cloud computing and digital payment services.Connectivity to the Yandex Cloud platform fell to around 30 per cent of normal levels following the October 8-11 strikes, The Moscow times reported, quoting internet monitoring group NetBlocks.Disruptions also affected third-party businesses that depend on its infrastructure, with users reporting problems accessing files, ordering taxis and entering residential buildings after digital keys stopped working.Yandex confirmed that one data centre had sustained significant damage, another had been shut down, and a third had suffered infrastructure disruptions.Although access to Yandex Pay was subsequently restored, several people reported that the service displayed an incorrect account balance.According to The Moscow Times, Yandex Pay remained only partially operational as of Monday, displaying a reassurance to users in place of the earlier error message: “Your money is safe. Some features are unavailable. Our engineers are working to get everything up and running again.”State agencies and private businesses relying on Yandex infrastructure, including dating apps and access systems for residential complexes and smart homes, also faced disruptions, The Moscow Times reported.Taxi drivers were also affected. Three drivers told NBC News they could not track their earnings or withdraw their money during the outage. One said the application had displayed error messages and, at times, dispatched multiple cars for a single customer.On October 14, Ukrainian drones struck a Sberbank data centre in the Saratov region. However, the bank said its systems remained operational.“We confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption,” Alexander Vedyakhin, Sberbank’s first deputy CEO told Reuters.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the government was discussing Yandex’s difficulties but that it was too early to assess whether users had suffered financial losses. Russia’s digital development minister Maksut Shadayev said officials were working with the defence ministry on measures to protect data centres, according to The Moscow Times.Ukraine has described the strikes as retaliation for Russian attacks on its own digital infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet”.The attacks have exposed the risks posed by Russia’s reliance on a relatively small number of major technology providers.Meanwhile, Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraine’s digital and energy infrastructure. However, Russian data centres were potentially more vulnerable because many are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, whereas Ukraine’s are more widely dispersed. A strike on a single Russian facility can therefore disrupt services spanning payments, transport and internet access.
Article Summary: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centres have disrupted banking, taxi services, food deliveries and digital access to homes. This comes as Kyiv expands its campaign against Moscow’s technology infrastructure. The attacks, carried out over several days in October, targeted data centres operated by Yandex.

Article Title: Explosion, fuel leak: Two Syrian pipelines damaged in fresh blow to war-hit energy network
Article Text:
Security forces of Syria's Interior Ministry guard the al-Omar oil field, the country's largest by area and production

Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday, with one explosion triggering a fire and another causing a fuel leak, Syrian state media reported.According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), citing the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, an explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in Hasakah province, while a separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.The explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze.The Syrian Petroleum Company described the incident as sabotage. Officials said alternative arrangements would maintain gas supplies to power stations during repairs, while domestic gas supplies remained unaffected.In a separate incident, a hole was discovered in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area west of Homs, causing a leak of petroleum products. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to contain the leak and isolate the damaged section.Al Jazeera, citing Syrian state media, reported that the damage to the Baniyas-Homs pipeline was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft. The initial reports did not confirm the cause or identify those responsible.The incidents come amid a series of disruptions to Syria’s energy infrastructure. Earlier in October, an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in Hasakah province was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage.Syria is working to rebuild its oil and gas infrastructure after years of conflict, restoring production in northeastern oilfields and reconnecting them with processing facilities and refineries in Homs and Baniyas.In January 2026, the Syrian Petroleum Company began pumping raw gas from the Jbessa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs countryside at around 1.2 million cubic metres per day to support electricity generation.The second damaged pipeline, connecting Baniyas on the Mediterranean coast to Homs, transports petroleum products between two important energy centres. The Baniyas refinery is undergoing an overhaul aimed at increasing its processing capacity from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.Syria has also undertaken emergency pipeline repairs and plans to expand its transportation network. A September 2026 analysis by the Baker Institute for Public Policy reported that the Syrian Petroleum Company was repairing existing infrastructure and planning a heavy-crude pipeline linking northeastern oilfields to the Baniyas refinery.
Article Summary: Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday. One explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze. A separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.
