Article Title: In a solar-simulator test, aluminum cooling fins raised a panel’s output 11.5%; adding folded plastic bags lifted the increase only slightly, to 11.6%
Article Text:
AI Representation: A photovoltaic panel fitted with aluminum cooling fins and folded plastic bags at the rear. Image credits: Chatgpt

Aluminum fins helped release heat from the panel

Investigation of Repurposed Material Utilization for Environmental Protection and Reduction of Overheat Power Losses in PV Panels

Aluminum fins and folded plastic bags increased output power by 11.6%

Lower panel temperatures can improve electrical performance

A real solar simulator in a university clean-energy laboratory. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Outdoor testing is needed to establish practical benefits

Solar panels can lose some of their electrical performance as they heat up under strong sunlight. Scientists have tried several ways to limit heat on panels without electric cooling, including using affordable materials that would normally be thrown away. One study used a cheap combination of aluminum heat sinks and folded plastic bags mounted on the rear of a solar panel. These results suggest that a non-electric cooling system can improve solar panel performance, at least under laboratory conditions. Discarded plastic bags could thus have another application in managing heat.A 2019 study by Ammar Alkhalidi, Mohamad K. Khawaja and Abdel Ghaffar Al Kelany,, published in the International Journal of Photoenergy , examined whether repurposed plastic materials could help cool photovoltaic panels and reduce heat-related power losses. The researchers tested the panel under halogen-lamp simulator conditions, then added fitted heat-extraction fins before layering in repurposed HDPE and plastic bags.They report that this passive cooling approach lowered panel temperature and raised power output at 1000 W m⁻², with the perforated fin design chosen for its lower weight and better airflow. The perforated aluminum fins were attached to the back of the panel to increase its surface area for heat exchange, and the perforations let air move through them.No fans or pumps were used because the cooling method was passive.The biggest performance increase came from combining aluminum cooling fins with folded plastic bags on the back of the panel. At a simulated irradiance of 1,000 watts per square metre, this configuration produced 11.6% more output power than the unmodified panel and lowered the panel’s temperature by 22.7%. Aluminum fins alone raised output power by 11.5%, so the bags added only a small further gain. The study also tested the fins with ground HDPE, but the highest output came from the folded plastic bags.Heat management matters because photovoltaic modules generally lose electrical performance as their operating temperature rises. The review On the temperature dependence of photovoltaic module electrical performance: A review of efficiency/power correlations by E. Skoplaki and J. A. Palyvos, published in Solar Energy in 2009, examines the relationship between module temperature, electrical efficiency, and power output. In the opinion of the authors, the review is dedicated to one-sun commercial silicon modules and considers how temperature affects the major electrical characteristics, particularly efficiency and maximum power. The review also emphasizes the typical test condition of 25°C and 1000 W/m² and explains the temperature effect using the well-known negative temperature coefficient.The energy production of solar panels requires sunlight, but the heat caused by high irradiance lowers their voltage and peak power. Thus, removal of excessive heat could enable a panel to produce more efficient electric energy using the same amount of sunlight. In the above-mentioned study by Alkhalidi and colleagues, the possibility was tested with a passive cooling system made of aluminum fins and plastic. Since this system did not use any equipment for active cooling, it had the potential to increase the efficiency of panels without requiring additional electricity consumption. But the observed effect was reached only in a laboratory setting, not necessarily reflecting results that could be achieved in outdoor installations due to variations in sunlight, air moisture, and wind.The combination of these materials with aluminum fins represents a simple way of temperature control and reuse of waste material. There are some practical issues that need to be investigated. For example, how does the change of outdoor conditions such as varying light, wind, dust, and humidity influence the cooling process? The researchers should study the system's durability, maintenance, and costs of its installation before determining its feasibility. This experiment showed that a passive cooling system using aluminum fins and folded plastic bags can increase a solar panel’s power under laboratory conditions.
Article Summary: Solar panels can lose some of their electrical performance as they heat up under strong sunlight. Scientists have tried several ways to limit heat on panels without electric cooling. One study used a cheap combination of aluminum heat sinks and folded plastic bags mounted on the rear of a solar panel. The results suggest that a non-electric cooling system can improve solar panel performance.

Article Title: In 1801, Paul Revere bought a home near Boston; 220 years later, renovators found a rare family sign in its attic, and the artifacts sold for $20,000
Article Text:
Paul Revere, the American silversmith and Revolutionary War figure whose family artifacts were discovered in Canton, Massachusetts | Wikimedia Commons. Right: The Paul Revere House in Boston, shown here as a representative image; it is not the Canton property where the artifacts were found | Library of Congress​

A

family trade sign

attracted bidders

Joseph W. Revere, Paul Revere's son | Wikimedia Commons

Why the Canton property mattered

Renovators were working on a house in Canton, Massachusetts, when they discovered a collection of artifacts that were associated with Paul Revere's family in an attic wall in 2021. The objects included a black trade sign that bore the name of Revere's son, Joseph W. Revere, along with letters, tools and personal belongings that were connected to the family. The collection was sold as a single lot by an auction house for $20,000 on December 11, 2021, which far exceeded the auctioneer's expectations. John McInnis had expected a sale that fell below $8,000, while the auction website estimated that the collection would fetch between $1,000 and $2,000.A trade sign that was painted black with gold-leaf lettering was one of the most prominent objects in the collection, which carried the name Joseph W. Revere, Paul Revere's son, and was believed to be linked with a business that was operated by the Revere family in Canton. The other objects included wrought-iron calipers, a turned wooden handle, a key, a sewing valet that was made from silk and leather, letters and an account book that belonged to Revere's descendants and daughter-in-law.The company that handled the auction was McInnis, who said that the objects had a historical connection that increased their value, with the auction attracting online, telephone and in-person bidders, and an unidentified online bidder ultimately winning the lot. McInnis told The Boston Globe that early American trade signs typically sold for between $500 and $5,000, based on their condition and appearance. He said that the association with the Revere family made the collection a lot more desirable.Paul Revere purchased a property in Canton in 1801, according to the Associated Press, and later established the Revere Copper Company on the land. The house where renovators found the objects was believed to have belonged to the Revere family. The artifacts were discovered behind a wall in the attic during renovation work, and their location had kept them out of view, although the available reports do not establish when they were placed there.The collection's historical connection linked the objects to a documented family rather than leaving them as unidentified antiques, which was important to the auction, and the trade sign, in particular, carried a name that could be associated with Revere's descendants. The National Park Service identifies Revere as a master silversmith, engraver, industrialist and messenger during the American Revolution, who became widely known for his ride on the night of April 18, 1775, when he helped warn Patriot leaders of the approaching British forces before the battles of Lexington and Concord. His work as an artisan and businessman continued after the Revolution.Revere’s later enterprises included a foundry and copper mill, with his industrial activities becoming an important part of his career, and the Canton property was connected to this phase of his life. The recovered collection belonged to a later period of the family's history, but its exact age and the circumstances that surrounded its storage were not established fully in the published accounts. The sign's association with Joseph W. Revere and the family documents helped auctioneers identify the lot's historical provenance.The winning bidder remained unidentified, and the reports did not specify where the artifacts would go after the sale. The auction concluded on December 11, 2021, almost two centuries after Revere purchased the Canton property. The objects had emerged during renovation work, and their family connections helped determine the price they ultimately fetched.
Article Summary: Renovators in Canton, Massachusetts, discovered a collection of artifacts associated with Paul Revere's family in an attic wall in 2021. The objects included a black trade sign that bore the name of Revere’s son, Joseph W. Revere, along with letters, tools and personal belongings that were connected to the family. The collection was sold as a single lot by an auction house for $20,000 on December 11, 2021, which far exceeded the auctioneer's expectations.

Article Title: In 2022, a fourth-generation Colorado farming family sold 90 acres to Xcel Energy for $585,000; four years later, the utility sought a 550-foot easement for $19,000, but a judge rejected its condemnat
Article Text:
A disagreement over the route and compensation

Why the disputed power lines matter

Colorado Supreme Court declines an early intervention

A dispute over a narrow strip of ranchland in eastern Colorado has become a broader legal battle over how far an electricity utility can go to secure land for renewable energy projects. According to reporting by The Colorado Sun, Utility Dive and the Kiowa County Independent, Xcel Energy is challenging a ruling that denied it the power to seize a disputed easement from a fourth-generation farming and ranching family. The conflict centres on Dryland Partners, a family-run agricultural business operated by Darin Dickey and his brothers in Cheyenne County. The family had sold approximately 90 acres to Xcel Energy in 2022 for $585,000 to accommodate the Goose Creek substation. However, negotiations later broke down over a separate 550-foot right of way needed to connect two wind farms to the electricity grid.In June 2026, Cheyenne County District Judge Mike Davidson rejected the utility’s condemnation petition, finding that it lacked the authority to acquire the land through eminent domain for the proposed generation tie lines. The judge also determined that the utility had acted in bad faith by pursuing a route that would cause unnecessary harm to the landowners despite the availability of less damaging alternatives.Xcel Energy, through its subsidiary Public Service Company of Colorado, proposed routing the power lines across the intersection of County Roads DD and 36 before connecting them to the Goose Creek substation.The Dickey family objected to this alignment, citing potential safety concerns for heavy agricultural machinery and possible interference with an existing natural gas pipeline right of way. The family proposed alternative routes that it said would reduce disruption to its farming operations. The utility offered $19,000 for the easement, an amount the family considered inadequate compared with compensation negotiated for a separate wind energy connection at the same substation. Dryland Partners had previously reached an agreement with NextEra Energy Resources to connect its Dusty Rose wind farm to the facility.Xcel maintained that its offer exceeded fair market value and argued that the family’s alternative proposals would involve prohibitively expensive changes. The disagreement over compensation, however, is only one part of the case. The central legal question is whether a regulated utility can use eminent domain to obtain land for generation tie lines that connect individual power plants to the grid.The easement is required for two wind projects, Singing Grass and Cheyenne Ridge II, which have a combined planned generating capacity of approximately 1,053 megawatts. The projects are intended to connect to the Goose Creek substation and subsequently feed electricity into Xcel’s $1.7 billion Power Pathway transmission network.The distinction between transmission infrastructure and generation tie lines is central to the dispute. While utilities have established authority to acquire certain land for public transmission infrastructure, the family argued that the disputed connections primarily serve individual generating facilities rather than directly delivering electricity to consumers. The ruling could therefore have implications beyond the Dickey family’s property, potentially influencing how renewable energy developers secure land for connections to the wider electricity network.Xcel sought to have the Colorado Supreme Court consider the case directly, arguing that the dispute raised important questions about renewable energy development and the utility’s condemnation powers. However, on August 31, 2026, the state’s highest court declined to take up the case through this expedited route. The decision did not resolve the underlying legal questions. Xcel said it would continue with its appeal before the Colorado Court of Appeals.The utility has argued that the unresolved easement is delaying the completion of infrastructure needed to bring the two wind farms online. The family, meanwhile, has maintained that it remains willing to negotiate a solution using alternative routes and reasonable terms. The outcome will determine more than the location of a power line across an agricultural property. It could also help clarify the limits of eminent domain when utilities seek land to connect privately developed or utility-owned renewable energy projects to the grid.
Article Summary: Colorado Supreme Court declines an early intervention in the case. The dispute centres on Dryland Partners, a family-run agricultural business operated by Darin Dickey and his brothers. The family had sold approximately 90 acres to Xcel Energy in 2022 for $585,000 to accommodate the Goose Creek substation.

Article Title: Built in 1938, Oklahoma's eight-storey Jim Thorpe Memorial Office Building underwent a three-year, $70 million restoration; officials unveiled its Art Deco interiors in October 2026, with agencies ret
Article Text:
Photo credit: Ben Bigler, OMES Outreach.

A historic building renewed

Art Deco details preserved

Designed for modern government

Agencies returning this winter

A tribute to Jim Thorpe

Oklahoma has unveiled the restored Art Deco interiors of the Jim Thorpe Memorial Office Building after a three-year, $70 million renovation of the eight-storey landmark in Oklahoma City. Built in 1938, the building has been modernised for public access, safety and agency operations while retaining signature features such as limestone walls, terrazzo floors, plaster ceilings and historic light fixtures. State leaders marked the completion with a ribbon-cutting on October 14, 2026, according to Oklahoma’s Office of Management and Enterprise Services. Read more details about it, as per the report, here:The Jim Thorpe Memorial Office Building has been part of Oklahoma’s Capitol Complex for more than eight decades. Originally called the State Capitol Office Building, it was renamed in 1961 in honour of Jim Thorpe, the Oklahoma-born Olympic athlete and one of the state’s most celebrated figures.By 2023, when the current renovation began, the building’s infrastructure needed extensive repair and modernisation. The project addressed long-standing problems including water infiltration, poor insulation and outdated layouts, while upgrading core building systems and installing energy-efficient windows designed to match the original appearance of the facade.The restoration was funded by state lawmakers through House Bill 1011X. Lawmakers also created the Jim Thorpe Repair Expenditure Oversight Committee through House Bill 1033X to review spending on interior and exterior repairs and provide public oversight as the work progressed through competitive procurement.The renovation focused as much on preservation as on modernisation. Project teams restored and protected defining Art Deco elements, including the building’s limestone walls, plaster ceilings, terrazzo floors and original light fixtures. These details help the renovated offices retain the architectural character of the late 1930s rather than becoming a generic government building.The building also retains important works of public art. In the lobby, 1930s-era bas-relief sculptures carved into the stone walls were carefully preserved, along with the exterior pediment sculpture above the east entrance. These works were co-created by Oklahoma art professors Doel Reed of Oklahoma State University and Joe Taylor of the University of Oklahoma, as per the report.New artworks were commissioned by the Oklahoma Arts Council under the state’s public art programme. The report also shares that Oklahoma artists Dr Jessica Moore Harjo and Erica Pretty Eagle Cozad created brass, copper and stainless steel ceiling installations for the first-floor corridors and sixth-floor elevator landing. Their designs use Sac and Fox motifs connected to the state flower, the state wildflower and the swan, a symbol of survival and resilience.The updated building is intended to make public services easier to access. Public-facing functions, including hearing and courtroom spaces, have been concentrated on the first floor, reducing confusion for visitors and improving accessibility.Behind the restored interiors, the renovation reconfigured older spaces for contemporary agency operations, public access and safety requirements. The eight-floor building now has the infrastructure needed to support modern state government while preserving the historic shell and architectural identity that make it distinctive.OMES Director Mark Wood said, according to the report, that the completed project honours the building’s historic character while providing the accessibility, infrastructure and functionality required for modern state government. He added that the agency was proud to guide the project from planning through completion.Four state agencies will occupy the renovated building: the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, Oklahoma Arts Council, State Election Board and Oklahoma Water Resources Board. Their work covers areas that affect daily life across Oklahoma, including utilities, elections, the arts and water resources.The agencies will move in in phases beginning this winter. Once they are settled, the Jim Thorpe Memorial Office Building will return to its role as a central hub for essential public services within the Capitol Complex.Jim Marshall, interim director of the Oklahoma Corporation Commission and chair of the repair oversight committee, said the investment would make the building easier to access, more inviting and better equipped for the work ahead. He noted that the renovation would benefit both the agencies moving in and the residents who rely on their services.For Thorpe’s family, the restored building carries a meaning beyond architecture and public administration. His granddaughter, Anita Thorpe, said it was deeply meaningful to see his name continue to be honoured in a place dedicated to public service, describing the building as a reflection of strength, perseverance and pride.The new public art also connects the building to Thorpe’s Sac and Fox heritage and his Olympic legacy. According to the Oklahoma Arts Council, the installations subtly reference his athletic achievements while linking the building’s past to Oklahoma’s present and future.The completed restoration shows how a historic government building can be brought up to modern standards without erasing the craftsmanship and cultural stories embedded in its walls. With its Art Deco interiors restored and agencies preparing to return, the Jim Thorpe Memorial Office Building is set to serve Oklahomans for another generation.
Article Summary: The Jim Thorpe Memorial Office Building has been part of Oklahoma’s Capitol Complex for more than eight decades. Originally called the State Capitol Office Building, it was renamed in 1961 in honour of the Oklahoma-born Olympic athlete. The renovation focused as much on preservation as on modernisation. The eight- floor building now has the infrastructure needed to support modern state government while preserving the historic shell.

Article Title: 'US is acting as international delinquent': Why Cuba and America clashed at UN
Article Text:
US and Cuba clash at UN over human rights and 60 year-old trade embargo

The United States and Cuba clashed at the United Nations on Monday after a US-hosted event brought together Cuban dissidents to discuss alleged human rights abuses by the nation’s government.The event, held at the UN building, ended with a heated exchange as Cuban ambassador Ernesto Soberón Guzmán and other Cuban representatives shouted at US ambassador Mike Waltz while he was leaving.The incident comes ahead of a UN General Assembly vote on a resolution calling for an end to the US trade embargo on Cuba. The vote is expected on October 27-28. The non-binding resolution has been passed by wide margins every year since 1992, but only the US Congress can lift the embargo.Speaking to reporters in New York, Waltz accused Cuban diplomats of harassing and intimidating former political prisoners who had recently been released, as well as other people attending the event."I hope you...noted the so-called diplomats from the Cuban embassy here that we allow here by dint of treaty, harassing, yelling, intimidating, and filming not only our just released former political prisoners but others," Waltz said.He also accused the Cuban government of using the annual UN resolution to defend its actions and hide the suffering of its people."Year after year, the Cuban regime comes to the General Assembly and propagates a lie through its annual resolution...It uses excuse after excuse to justify its oppression, to justify the misery of the Cuban people, and what we are doing here at the US mission to the UN is exposing those lies," he said.Guzmán, meanwhile, accused Washington of worsening the hardships faced by ordinary Cubans through its sanctions. Speaking at an impromptu gathering outside the US meeting with dissidents, he said the restrictions amounted to collective punishment."The US is acting as an international delinquent, enforcing collective punishment on the people of Cuba. They are inflicting immense suffering upon the whole population of a peaceful nation," Guzmán said.The exchange comes as tensions between the two countries grow amid a US-imposed oil blockade on Cuba. Washington has maintained a trade embargo on the island for more than 60 years, with US President Donald Trump's administration increasing pressure on the country after using the military in January to remove Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.Cuba has blamed US sanctions for its deepening economic crisis, which has brought shortages of basic goods, failing infrastructure and runaway inflation. The country is facing its worst economic downturn in decades.Last month, Trump told the UN that Cuba was a failed state and said freedom would be coming to the island.The country's crisis has also affected its power supply. Cuba's electrical grid suffered a total collapse last month, leaving millions of people without electricity.
Article Summary: US-hosted event brought together Cuban dissidents to discuss alleged human rights abuses. US ambassador Mike Waltz accused Cuban diplomats of harassing and intimidating former political prisoners. The incident comes ahead of a UN General Assembly vote on a resolution calling for an end to the US trade embargo.

Article Title: A 10-year-old held a 6-year-old boy dangling from a chairlift about 16 feet above the ground for 4 minutes; he has now received the Carnegie Medal
Article Text:
Representative Image of presenting the Carnegie Medal to a brave young boy (AI-generated image)

How Major Metzger held a 6-year-old boy above the ground

Carnegie Medal: what the civilian heroism award recognises

Major Metzger receives the Carnegie Medal in September 2026

What the chairlift rescue shows

A ski trip in Virginia took an unexpected turn on Jan. 26, 2025, when a 6-year-old boy slipped off a moving chairlift and dangled above rough, sloping ground. Sitting beside him was Major Metzger, then 10, who grabbed the younger boy’s arms and held on until ski patrol reached them with a safety mat. The chair was about 16 feet above the ground, and the boy remained suspended for approximately 4 minutes. He eventually fell onto the mat, suffering a small bump on his head, and did not require further medical treatment. Metzger’s actions have since earned him the Carnegie Medal, one of North America’s highest honours for civilian heroism. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger presented the medal to him in September 2026, formally recognising a rescue that began with a child trying to keep his friend from falling.According to the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission, the incident happened at a ski resort in Nellysford, Virginia, on Jan. 26, 2025. Six-year-old Bryce Rader was boarding a 4-person chairlift with 3 other children, including Metzger and their sisters. As the lift began moving uphill, Rader struggled to sit securely with his ski equipment. His helmet and skis added to the difficulty as he began sliding off the seat. Metzger, seated immediately beside him, grabbed him and tried to pull him back onto the chair.Workers were alerted and attempted to stop the lift, but Rader had already fallen completely off the seat by the time it came to a full stop. The bottom of the chair was about 16 feet above rugged, sloping ground.Metzger leaned forward and down, holding Rader’s arms with both gloved hands. He was wearing a helmet and skis himself, making the position particularly difficult as he tried to keep the younger boy from falling. He continued holding Rader while ski patrol made its way beneath the chair with a safety mat. Once rescuers were in position, they instructed Metzger to let go. Rader fell onto the mat and bounced off it, sustaining a small bump on his head. Medical staff evaluated him, but he did not need additional treatment and recovered. Metzger also made it safely off the lift. His arms were sore and he was shaken by the experience, although he did not require medical treatment. The Carnegie Hero Fund’s account documents the sequence of events, from Rader’s difficulty boarding to the moment ski patrol positioned the mat. It does not suggest that Metzger had time to plan his response. He acted as the situation unfolded and continued holding on until rescuers could reach the children.The Carnegie Hero Fund Commission describes the Carnegie Medal as North America’s highest honour for civilian heroism. It recognises people in the United States and Canada who risk death or serious physical injury to an extraordinary degree while saving, or attempting to save, another person. The award is administered by the Pittsburgh-based Carnegie Hero Fund Commission, established by industrialist and philanthropist Andrew Carnegie in 1904. On March 24, 2026, the commission announced 18 new medal recipients, including Metzger. The announcement described the recognised acts as involving people who risked serious injury or death, or were killed, while trying to save others. The people saved by recipients in that round included 11 children.The Carnegie Hero Fund Commission’s latest award announcement puts the total number of Carnegie Medal recipients at 10,597 since the fund was established in 1904. The commission also reports that more than $47 million has been distributed through one-time grants, scholarship aid, death benefits and continuing assistance. The award is not limited to professional rescuers. Its purpose is to recognise extraordinary civilian acts in which people place themselves in danger to protect others. Metzger’s case illustrates how such an act can occur in an everyday setting, without specialist equipment or time to prepare.Other people recognised in the March 2026 announcement included Sean Hayes, a 33-year-old teacher who helped rescue a 15-year-old student set on fire at a school in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and Matt Vasey, a 54-year-old man who pulled the pilot from a floatplane that flipped over and crashed in a lake in Bellevue, Washington. The pilot later died from his injuries. The commission publishes individual citations describing the circumstances of each rescue, as well as information about its award consideration process.The medal announcement was not the final recognition of Metzger’s actions. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger presented Metzger with the Carnegie Medal in Virginia Beach on Sept. 16, 2026, according to a news release published by the governor’s office on Sept. 17. Spanberger praised Metzger’s courage, saying his actions represented the best of Virginia. The ceremony was attended by members of his family, school officials and local leaders.The presentation recognised an event that had occurred more than a year earlier, when Metzger was still 10. The official citation identifies Rader as the child he saved and records the date and location of the chairlift incident. The Carnegie Medal’s recognition of Metzger places his actions among a long history of civilian rescues involving fires, accidents, drowning incidents and other emergencies. In this case, the danger developed quickly, and the child who intervened was also exposed to the risk of falling.The incident highlights how quickly a routine ski outing can become an emergency, particularly when a young child struggles to sit securely on a moving lift. It also shows the importance of trained ski patrol teams and rescue equipment: patrol members brought a safety mat beneath the chair and directed the moment when Metzger should release his grip. The official account does not assign blame to the children or their families. Instead, it records how Metzger responded to his friend’s predicament and how rescuers helped bring the incident to a safe conclusion.For families, the practical lesson is to follow the individual resort’s chairlift instructions, ask lift staff for assistance when a child needs help boarding, and take concerns about a child’s ability to ride safely seriously. Specific procedures can vary by resort, so families should consult the resort’s own guidance rather than assume that one set of instructions applies everywhere. Metzger’s actions were recognised because he continued holding Rader until trained help was in position. His Carnegie Medal formally recognises the actions of a 10-year-old who held on to another child until ski patrol could assist.
Article Summary: Major Metzger, then 10, held a 6-year-old boy above the ground on a chairlift. The chair was about 16 feet above rough, sloping ground. He held on until ski patrol reached them with a safety mat. The boy eventually fell onto the mat, suffering a small bump on his head. His actions have earned him the Carnegie Medal, one of North America’s highest honours for civilian heroism.

Article Title: Two Indians among 28 green card holders charged with election fraud in California
Article Text:
1. Two Indians face US election fraud charges over 2024 voting (Representative image: Reuters photo)

Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with election-related offences in California, including fraudulent voter registration and voting in the November 2024 US elections, the US Department of Justice said on Monday.The accused Indians have been identified as Amandeep Kaur, 30, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, who lives in Sacramento. It was not immediately clear whether either of them was among the 11 people arrested during early morning raids across California under ‘Operation Protect the Vote’.According to the Justice Department, Shah fraudulently registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast his ballot the same day. Kaur, who is seeking US citizenship, allegedly registered to vote in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 election.“All 28 foreign nationals charged are lawful permanent residents (LPRs), or 'green card' holders. Although LPRs have legal immigration status in the United States, they are not US citizens and are not permitted to vote in US elections,” the Justice Department said.The charges include making false statements in naturalisation applications and fraudulent voter registration.Both offences are felonies that carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison.DOJ links accused to voter registration listActing Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said all 28 defendants appeared on a list of more than 20,000 people the Justice Department had provided to California election officials the previous week.“Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week,” McCotter told reporters in Los Angeles.The charges come amid an escalating dispute between the Trump administration and California officials over allegations of non-citizen voter registration. The Justice Department has also asked a federal court to prevent California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots returned by people on the list, arguing that votes cast illegally could undermine election integrity.California officials have opposed the demand, saying the federal government has not provided sufficient evidence to establish that those listed are non-citizens. They have also argued that withholding or refusing to count ballots could violate federal and state law and disenfranchise eligible voters.Trump administration steps up election investigationsThe Justice Department has intensified investigations into alleged election-related offences as early voting begins in several states. Before Monday’s announcement, it had charged about 90 people with various forms of election misconduct this year, including 50 accused of voting as non-citizens.The department said on Monday that it had charged 113 non-citizens across 20 states with voting and registration offences over the preceding seven weeks.Election law experts have cautioned that such cases do not establish widespread non-citizen voting. They have also warned that aggressive efforts to scrutinise voter rolls could risk removing eligible voters or undermining public confidence in elections.California officials have questioned the Justice Department’s methodology for identifying the 20,000 people, while the federal government has argued that access to additional voter registration data would help verify their citizenship status.
Article Summary: Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with election- related offences in California. The accused Indians have been identified as Amandeep Kaur, 30, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, who lives in Sacramento. The charges include making false statements in naturalisation applications and fraudulent voter registration.

Article Title: ‘US will burn like France’: Trump unleashes anti-immigrant tirade in bid to boost Republicans
Article Text:
Trump blames immigration for France protests

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think should be the top priority for the upcoming elections? Economic Issues Immigration Policies Cultural Issues Healthcare 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

US President Donald Trump invoked violent unrest in France to attack Democrats and rally support for Republican Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas, warning that similar scenes could unfold in the United States if his political opponents prevail in the November 3 midterm elections.Earlier, Trump claimed he had warned French president Emmanuel Macron to close France’s borders, saying Paris would otherwise become a “Muslim city”.At a rally on Monday evening, Trump blamed immigration for the unrest in France, where protests over rising cost of living and declining purchasing power escalated into looting and clashes with police in several cities, according to Reuters.“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” Trump told the crowd.He described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists".“We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said. “When you see burning steeples and ⁠raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.”Speaking to reporters outside the White House earlier on Monday, Trump repeated his criticism of French president Emmanuel Macron’s immigration policies, claiming he had warned him years ago to tighten border controls.“Emanuel is a friend of mine. I told him a long time ago, ‘You’re making a big mistake in France. You’re letting everybody from the world come in. The whole world was coming in. Paris was going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal. That wasn’t the deal.’ I told him he should close up his borders. I’ve known him for eight or nine years, and I told him as soon as I met him,” Trump said.“Well, France, it is a very sad situation what’s happening in France, because what’s happening in France has to do with immigration, not schools, not anything. It’s immigration,” he said.Comparing France’s border policies with those of the United States, he said earlier, “I said you’re making a big mistake. We closed our borders; he didn’t. And you know what? His borders are a problem, and he also has a little bit of a problem with energy. But they are doing better than others. Emanuel should have closed his borders a long time ago. I told him to do it,” Trump told reporters.Nationwide demonstrations in France were called over the cost of living and pressure on household purchasing power. Reports of looting, fire and clashes prompted arrests and additional security measures, although the unrest’s causes extend beyond immigration.Trump’s remarks came as he campaigned for Marshall, who faces a competitive challenge from Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Kansas, a conservative Midwestern state that Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. Economic discontent and opposition to Trump’s tariff policies have complicated the Republican incumbent’s re-election campaign, Reuters reported.Trump has also mocked Democrats by calling them “Dumocrats”. At the rally, Trump attacked Hamilton, saying, “He wants you to repent for being born White.” Marshall, meanwhile, criticised his opponent over cultural issues, calling him “too woke”.Economic concerns remain a challenge for Republicans ahead of the midterms. A Reuters-Ipsos poll published on Monday put Trump’s approval rating at 31 per cent, its lowest level in the survey.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump blamed immigration for the unrest in France. He warned that similar scenes could unfold in the United States if his political opponents prevail in the November 3 midterm elections. Trump claimed he had warned French president Emmanuel Macron to close France’s borders, saying Paris would otherwise become a ‘Muslim city’

Article Title: Maryland landowners refused access to their properties for a 67-mile power-line project; appeals court upholds order allowing surveys before state approval
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Why Maryland landowners challenged access for a major power-line project

Why Maryland flagged PSEG’s power-line application

A US appeals court has upheld an order allowing PSEG Renewable Transmission LLC to access private properties in Maryland to conduct surveys for its proposed 67-mile Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, despite opposition from landowners and pending state approval. According to the Fourth Circuit, the Arentz Family and 116 other property owners refused access. The project’s application for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity remained administratively incomplete because required field studies had not been completed. The court backed survey access before final approval, while the Maryland Public Service Commission’s review of the project remained ongoing.PSEG is developing the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, a high-voltage transmission line intended to supply electricity to Maryland and the surrounding region. According to the Fourth Circuit's judgment, the proposed line would extend approximately 67 miles across Baltimore County, Carroll County and Frederick County. The project was selected by PJM Interconnection, the regional transmission organisation, following a 2023 solicitation for proposals to address growing electricity demand and the retirement of power-generation facilities.The dispute involved the Arentz Family and 116 other defendant-appellants who refused to allow PSEG onto their properties. The court record states that the affected land included multi-generational farms, properties subject to forest and wetland conservation easements, and land used for commercial businesses. PSEG sought access to carry out surveys needed to assess the project's environmental and socioeconomic effects and support its application for state approval.Maryland requires a transmission-line developer to obtain a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) from the Maryland Public Service Commission before construction can begin. PSEG submitted its application in December 2024, and the commission referred the question of completeness to the state's Power Plant Research Program (PPRP), part of the Maryland Department of Natural Resources.In March 2025, the PPRP reported that it lacked sufficient information to determine whether the application was complete. PSEG had submitted desktop studies based on secondary sources because it could not access the properties, but the programme said those studies could not be verified and that field studies were necessary. The application was consequently classified as “administratively incomplete”. The court record states that the PPRP estimated it would take approximately 30 months to assess a CPCN application after filing.
Article Summary: PSEG is developing the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, a high-voltage transmission line intended to supply electricity to Maryland and the surrounding region. The dispute involved the Arentz Family and 116 other defendant- appellants who refused to allow PSEG onto their properties.

Article Title: Donald Trump approval rating hits record low of 31% as midterms near, Democrats lead by 12 points
Article Text:
Donald Trump approval ratings: About three-quarters of Democratic voters say that voting in this November’s midterm elections is “extremely” important, compared with roughly 6 in 10 Republicans.

Women voters drive shift towards democrats

US President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31%, with rising gasoline prices and concerns over the economy weighing on public sentiment ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that concluded on Monday.The four-day survey found that Trump's approval rating dropped by one percentage point from two weeks earlier, marking the lowest level of either of his presidential terms. The poll also showed Democrats opening a 12-point lead over Republicans among registered voters, the widest margin recorded during the current election cycle.Asked which party they would support if congressional elections were held today, 47% of registered voters chose Democrats, compared with 35% who backed Republicans.The Democratic lead has widened from seven percentage points in the previous Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted two weeks earlier, when Democrats had 44% support against 37% for Republicans.However, national polls do not capture all the nuances of state-level Senate races and district-level House contests, where Republicans retain some structural advantages.The widening Democratic lead was partly driven by a larger share of women saying they would vote for Democratic candidates.Around 50% of female voters backed Democrats, compared with 32% who said they would vote Republican.Men also favoured Democrats, although the gap between the two parties was narrower among male voters.Trump's popularity has suffered since he ordered military strikes on Iran in February alongside US ally Israel. The war triggered a surge in gasoline prices, putting additional pressure on household finances.The poll found that 68% of Americans disapproved of Trump's handling of the economy. The figure included 37% of respondents who identified themselves as Republicans.When asked which party would do a better job managing the economy, 40% of respondents chose Democrats, compared with 33% who favoured Republicans.
Article Summary: Women voters drive shift towards democrats. Poll also showed Democrats opening a 12-point lead over Republicans. About three-quarters of Democratic voters say that voting in this November’s midterm elections is “extremely” important, compared with roughly 6 in 10 Republicans.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer killed in IED blast during Balochistan operation
Article Text:
Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists.

A Pakistan Army major was killed in an improvised explosive device (IED) blast during a security operation in Balochistan province, while security forces killed four terrorists in a separate operation, the military said on Monday.According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, security forces conducted operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Gwadar and Jattakabad in Kalat district on Sunday following reports of terrorist presence.During an operation in Jattakabad, the forces killed four terrorists and recovered “a large cache of arms and ammunition”, the Army said.In a separate action, security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district. During the operation, 34-year-old Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation.“Sanitisation operations will continue to eliminate any other terrorists found in the area,” the Army said.The military added that security forces and law enforcement agencies remained committed to eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism in the country.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for killing the four terrorists and expressed grief over the death of the officer.“Major Wajahat Waheed sacrificed his life for the protection of our beloved homeland; the nation is proud of its brave son,” the prime minister said.Sharif also extended condolences to the officer's family and prayed for the elevation of his rank.Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, with security forces continuing operations to contain the violence.A day earlier, security forces killed eight terrorists during operations in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts.(With inputs from PTI)
Article Summary: Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists. Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation. Security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district.

Article Title: US-designated LeT terrorist dies after mysteriously falling from building in Lahore
Article Text:
LeT terrorist Chaudhary Muhammed Sarwar.

NEW DELHI: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim, one of the founding members of the outfit, died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday.The incident reminded of a similar death that had occurred in 2016 when fake currency kingpin, Javed Khanani, had died after falling from an under construction building in Karachi.Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League. He was a close aide of both Hafiz Saeed and current deputy chief Saifullah Kasuri. Sarwar's son had also died in a road accident a few months ago.It was in 2016 tha Sarwar was designated a terrorist by the US justice department who termed himself as a senior LeT memeber in Lahore active since early 2000s, holding various leadership roles in the group. At the time, he was LeT’s emir for Lahore, a position he has held since at least January 2015."As the LeT emir of Lahore, Sarwar maintains relationships with LeT’s most senior leaders. Between 2012 and 2013, Sarwar worked with LeT’s foreign affairs chief Hafiz Abdul Rahman Makki, and in early 2013, Makki asked Sarwar for money to pay for his travel within Pakistan," the US justice department had said in its statement."Sarwar had been directly involved in LeT fundraising activities and used the formal financial system in Pakistan to raise and move funds on behalf of LeT. For example, in 2008, Sarwar led delegations of businessmen to LeT facilities for the purpose of soliciting donations for the group," it added.
Article Summary: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday. Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League.

Article Title: Pakistani forces kill 8 militants in Balochistan, raid hideouts as abductions rise
Article Text:
The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas (Photo: ANI).

Pakistani security forces on Sunday reportedly killed eight militants in three intelligence-led operations across districts of Balochistan province, amid rising cases of abduction in the troubled region.The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas, according to the Inter Service Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of the Pakistan Army.In the Panjpai area of Quetta district, terrorists trying to set up a roadblock to disrupt local traffic were "intercepted by security forces, resulting in [the] killing of five terrorists", the ISPR said in a statement.In Nushki district, security forces stormed a hideout, and two terrorists were killed in an intense exchange of fire, the army said. Around 500 kilograms of explosives were also recovered from the terrorists during that operation. In Khuzdar district, one terrorist was killed, the ISPR added.Balochistan, which borders Afghanistan, has seen a surge in abductions and attacks on civilians and securityforces in recent years, prompting the government to step up its anti-militant operations.On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers near Mastung, on the Quetta-Karachi highway, and took them away. Their whereabouts remain unknown.On Sunday, at least 18 workers were abducted, and another was injured when unidentified armed men attacked a marble mining site in the province. The incident happened early in the morning in the remote Naal area of Khuzdar district, police said. The attackers arrived on motorcycles and other vehicles and stormed the site.According to PTI, no insurgent group or individual has claimed responsibility for the attack.The police and the provincial government have yet to confirm the incident officially, but two police officers, speaking on condition of anonymity, said 18 workers had been taken away by the attackers. PTI reported."They came on bikes and vehicles and opened fire and then rounded up the workers present at the site and abducted 18 of them before fleeing," a police officer said.Most of those abducted came from nearby villages and areas, he added, and another worker was injured in the attack.
Article Summary: Pakistani security forces reportedly kill eight militants in three intelligence- led operations across districts of Balochistan province. Operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas. On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers.

Article Title: Pakistan’s decades of backing terror comes full circle as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa falls under emergency rule
Article Text:
The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.

Decades of militant policy and blowback

Emergency rule and the erosion of elected authority

Opposition crackdown deepens rights concerns

Tribal communities face renewed uncertainty

Pakistan’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11 has placed the province under direct federal control. It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The move, which invokes Articles 232 and 234 of the Pakistani Constitution, comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. It has also renewed questions over Pakistan’s decades-long policy of using militant groups for strategic gains. A report by news agency ANI highlights how this policy has fuelled the violence now threatening its own territory.The emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, further weakening elected authority in a province that has long borne the consequences of Pakistan’s security policies. The move follows years of political turmoil, including Khan’s imprisonment, constitutional amendments that have weakened judicial independence, and the removal of the PTI-led provincial government.The concentration of power in unelected authorities, alongside the military’s expanding role in civilian affairs, has raised concerns over the state of democracy in Pakistan, according to a report by news agency ANI.Pakistan’s security crisis has deep roots in its long-standing use of militant groups as instruments of state policy. For more than five decades, the country has pursued strategic depth through its relationship with armed groups, while distinguishing between factions considered useful and those viewed as threats.This approach has contributed to a cycle of violence that has increasingly turned inward.As stated in the report, the state has repeatedly shifted its position towards militant organisations, including groups hostile to its own security forces. During former army chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa’s tenure, cadres of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were relocated to parts of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The consequences have proved difficult to contain. Pakistan’s struggle with militancy has exposed the risks of treating armed groups as strategic assets while assuming their violence can be directed towards selected targets.Former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton captured this danger in a widely cited remark, “one cannot rear snakes in a backyard and expect them to bite only neighbours, as they will eventually turn on their keepers”.Rather than confronting the broader implications of this policy, Pakistan has continued to differentiate between militant factions it considers acceptable and those it seeks to eliminate. The resulting security failures have placed civilians, particularly in the tribal areas, at the centre of a prolonged conflict.The imposition of emergency rule marks another stage in the concentration of power within Pakistan’s security establishment. The federal intervention has effectively displaced the PTI-led provincial administration, depriving the opposition of its remaining provincial government.The move follows Khan’s incarceration and constitutional changes that have curtailed judicial independence and shielded military leadership from accountability. Critics argue that these developments have weakened the institutions meant to limit executive and military power.The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.Instead of addressing the failures behind the province’s deteriorating security situation, authorities have expanded federal and military involvement in civilian administration. The move has intensified concerns that emergency powers are being used not only to manage the security crisis but also to consolidate political control.The intervention has been accompanied by a wider crackdown on the opposition. Leaders and legislators have been detained, residences raided and political demonstrations suppressed. Protesters have faced police firing, tear gas and mass arrests.The treatment of political opponents has fuelled concerns that dissent is increasingly being treated as a security threat. The use of force against protesters has also raised questions about the government’s claim that extraordinary measures are needed to restore law and order.The crackdown comes amid concerns over restrictions on reporting from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following earlier developments in Khyber before a blanket media ban was imposed on events in the province. Such restrictions risk limiting public scrutiny of security operations and their impact on civilians.The growing concentration of authority has therefore created a parallel crisis. While the state faces a persistent militant threat, its response has further narrowed the space for political opposition and public dissent.The latest intervention has also placed additional pressure on communities that have endured years of displacement and insecurity. Past military operations, including Zarb-e-Azb and Radd-ul-Fasad, remain associated with civilian hardship and human rights concerns.Thousands of displaced families are still awaiting return and rehabilitation. For these communities, the emergency raises fears of another period of disruption, particularly as the authorities expand their control and military involvement in civilian affairs.The consequences of Pakistan’s security policies have thus extended beyond the fight against armed groups. Tribal populations have faced displacement, civilian casualties and prolonged instability, while the failure to resolve the underlying conflict has left many vulnerable to further intervention.The emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa brings these tensions into sharper focus. A state that has long relied on militant groups to pursue strategic objectives now faces the consequences of violence within its own borders. Its response, however, has centred on expanding federal control, weakening elected authority and restricting opposition activity.Rather than resolving the crisis, the latest measures risk deepening the divide between the state and the communities it claims to protect. The removal of an elected provincial government, the concentration of power in unelected institutions and the crackdown on dissent point to a broader struggle over Pakistan’s democratic future, even as the country confronts the long-term fallout of its militant policies.
Article Summary: Emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) It comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers.

Article Title: Pakistan plans Moon landing by 2035, expands space cooperation with China
Article Text:
Pakistan sets 2035 Moon landing target as space programme expands, minister says (representative image)

First Pakistani astronaut to travel to China’s space station

Pakistan-China cooperation extends to lunar exploration

Space education and proposed museum

India’s space roadmap: From Gaganyaan to a Moon landing

Pakistan aims to land on the Moon by 2035 as it expands its space programme, planning minister Ahsan Iqbal said on Sunday, announcing that the country's first astronaut would embark on a space mission from China on November 25.Addressing the concluding ceremony of World Space Week 2026 in Narowal district of Punjab province, Iqbal said cooperation with China would help Pakistan advance its space exploration ambitions.Pakistan’s “first astronaut will embark on a space mission from China’s space centre on November 25, while the country aims to achieve a lunar landing by 2035,” he said, according to news agency PTI.The minister highlighted the growing role of space technology in agriculture, communications, climate monitoring, education and national security. He stressed that scientific research and space exploration were important for technological advancement.The upcoming mission is part of wider cooperation between Pakistan and China in space science and technology. According to Reuters, two Pakistani candidates, pilots Khurram Daud and Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, have been undergoing training in China, with one expected to be selected for the flight.The selected astronaut will serve as a payload specialist aboard China's Tiangong space station, conducting scientific experiments rather than operating the spacecraft, Reuters reported last month.Pakistan's space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), signed an agreement with the China Manned Space Agency in February 2025 to prepare a Pakistani astronaut for the mission, according to The Express Tribune.The two candidates had been training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Centre in Beijing, learning spacecraft systems, Mandarin and the physical demands of spaceflight.The mission is expected to last about a week. The astronaut will travel aboard a Chinese spacecraft launched from China and return to Earth with members of a Chinese crew.Pakistan does not have an independent launch vehicle or crewed spacecraft, making the mission dependent on China's space infrastructure and training facilities.Beyond the human spaceflight programme, Pakistan and China are collaborating on a Pakistani-built lunar rover planned for China's Chang'e-8 mission, expected around 2028.The rover is intended to use artificial intelligence-based stereo imaging to identify obstacles, assess distances and navigate the lunar surface autonomously, as direct real-time control from Earth would not be possible.However, Pakistan's participation in the lunar rover project is separate from its stated ambition to land on the Moon by 2035.According to Reuters, a Pakistani space agency official last month had said there was no official commitment or discussion about sending a Pakistani astronaut to the Moon under the existing partnership.Iqbal was speaking at the conclusion of World Space Week 2026, which was celebrated in Narowal for the first time in collaboration with SUPARCO. The event aimed to raise awareness among young people about space science, scientific research and modern technology.The minister also announced plans to establish Pakistan's first Space Museum at the University of Narowal to promote scientific awareness and encourage students to pursue careers in space science and technology.He said improved access to higher education was allowing students who had previously faced financial barriers to perform well academically.Iqbal congratulated the University of Narowal on securing first position at the Islamabad Science Festival, saying the achievement reflected the talent and potential of Pakistan's youth.The minister said the proposed museum would further encourage young people to explore scientific fields and pursue opportunities in space research and technology.India has also been advancing its space programme, with plans to send astronauts into orbit, establish its own space station and land an Indian on the Moon by 2040.According to the Union government’s roadmap outlined in Parliament in August, the first uncrewed Gaganyaan mission, carrying the humanoid robot Vyommitra, is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. Two further uncrewed missions are planned before India attempts its first crewed orbital flight, targeted by 2027.India also plans to establish the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035. The proposed station will comprise five modules, with the development and launch of its first module already approved.The longer-term goal is to send an Indian astronaut to the Moon by 2040.Other planned missions include Chandrayaan-4, which is intended to demonstrate technologies for returning lunar samples to Earth, and a Venus Orbiter Mission to study the planet’s surface, subsurface and atmosphere.These projects form part of India’s broader Space Vision 2047, which aims to expand its human spaceflight capabilities and deepen its role in space exploration.
Article Summary: Pakistan's first astronaut will embark on a space mission from China on November 25. Ahsan Iqbal said cooperation with China would help Pakistan advance its space exploration ambitions. Pakistan and China are collaborating on a Pakistani-built lunar rover planned for China's Chang'e-8 mission, expected around 2028.

Article Title: Balochistan unrest: Teacher's killing sparks outrage, kin say Pak officials shielding 'death squads'
Article Text:
What are Balochistan's 'death squads'?

(With ANI inputs)

The alleged torture and killing of a teacher in Pakistan’s restive Balochistan province triggered protests by his family members and local residents, who warned that a key highway would be blockaded if authorities failed to take action.The protesters accused Pakistani forces of shielding those allegedly responsible for the death of Parvez Mazar, an Arabic teacher at Government High School Babbar Shor in Pasni, a coastal town in Balochistan’s Gwadar district, The Balochistan Post reported.According to Mazar’s relatives, he was "taken away" in front of his family on Tuesday and was found dead the following day. They claimed that members of a state-backed armed group, described as a “death squad,” took him to a private torture facility, where he was detained and killed.Protesters, including Mazar’s children, gathered outside the Pasni Press Club, demanding the immediate arrest of those responsible for his death. They demanded accountability and justice for the deceased teacher's family.The demonstrators warned that failure to address their demands would prompt them to stage a sit-in at Pasni Zero Point and block the Makran Coastal Highway, a key route connecting Gwadar with Karachi in Sindh province, Pakistan’s largest city and the country's financial and commercial hub.They demanded that state institutions take action against armed groups accused of abducting, torturing and killing civilians while allegedly operating under the protection of state agencies.Baloch rights organisations and activists use the term “death squads” to describe armed groups they allege receive support or protection from Pakistani state institutions.These groups have been accused of targeting civilians, political activists and human rights defenders in Balochistan, a province long affected by an insurgency and a security crackdown.
Article Summary: Pervez Mazar, an Arabic teacher at Government High School Babbar Shor in Pasni, a coastal town in Balochistan’s Gwadar district, was found dead the following day. His family claimed that members of a state-backed armed group, described as a “death squad,” took him to a private torture facility, where he was detained and killed.

Article Title: Strong 6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan

6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan

More details awaited

An earthquake measuring 6.0 in magnitude struck southern Pakistan near Khuzdar, Balochistan on Saturday, around 95 km south of Sūrāb, according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC).The German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) said the earthquake struck at a depth of 10 km (6 miles).
