Article Title: Imran Khan facing Nawaz, Benazir-style exile deal? Pakistan opposition leader's big claim
Article Text:
Imran Khan

What happened in Nawaz Sharif, Benazir Bhutto's exile cases?

Achakzai demands access to prisoners, empowered parliament

Opposition challenges governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Pakistan opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai has claimed that jailed former prime minister Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to arrangements that led former premiers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto into exile, according to a report by Dawn published on Saturday.Achakzai, chairman of the Pakhtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PkMAP) and leader of the opposition in Pakistan's National Assembly, made the claim at a news conference at the Peshawar high court on Friday. He alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) were involved in a similar political arrangement.“The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Achakzai said, according to Dawn.The claim comes amid political tensions surrounding Imran Khan, founder of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), who remains in prison, and opposition allegations over restrictions on political activity and the functioning of elected institutions.Achakzai was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. He said opposition parties were in contact and that a multi-party conference would be convened soon.He also said resigning from the assemblies remained an option, adding that the opposition had submitted its demands in response to an offer of negotiations.Achakzai's remarks referred to the circumstances in which Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, two of Pakistan's most prominent former prime ministers, spent periods outside the country following political upheavals, Dawnreported.Sharif was ousted and imprisoned after a military coup led by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf. He left Pakistan in 2000 under a deal negotiated with the involvement of Saudi and Lebanese leaders.Bhutto, meanwhile, went into self-imposed exile after her Pakistan Peoples Party lost the 1997 general elections, following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leghari. Her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, was imprisoned on corruption charges and was released in 2004.Achakzai's comparison suggests that he believes a similar arrangement could be pursued in Khan's case. However, his remarks, as reported by Dawn, did not establish that an exile agreement involving the PTI founder had been reached.During the news conference, Achakzai criticised restrictions on prisoners' access to meetings and called for changes to what he described as a "wrong amendment". He also demanded that parliament be empowered and an independent commission be established to ensure transparent elections.“Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, according to Dawn.He argued that political disputes could not be resolved without strengthening parliament. He also expressed concern over the whereabouts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's chief minister and other lawmakers, demanding that the authorities disclose the chief minister's location.“We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived.Mengal, who accompanied Achakzai, criticised the government's actions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and questioned the imposition of governor's rule on grounds of terrorism. He also alleged that elected representatives had been displaced and questioned the legitimacy of the political system.Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, also criticised the situation, saying: “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” according to Dawn.Separately, TTAP leaders approached the Peshawar High Court on Friday, challenging the proclamation of emergency and the imposition of governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to Dawn, the petitioners asked the court to declare the October 11 proclamation, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of Pakistan's Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority. They argued that the constitutional conditions required for imposing the measures had not been met or that the government had exceeded its powers.The petition also challenged the purported transfer of the provincial assembly's legislative powers to parliament, the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet, and the establishment of the proposed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat.The petitioners sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications linked to the proclamation, including the deployment of armed forces to the extent that it allegedly violated constitutional requirements.They also requested interim relief to prevent the displacement of elected institutions and restrictions on elected representatives while the court considers the case.The legal challenge adds to the opposition's broader campaign against federal intervention in the province, as Achakzai seeks to bring opposition parties together over constitutional issues, political rights and negotiations with the government.
Article Summary: Mahmood Khan Achakzai claims Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to those that led Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto into exile. He claims the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) are involved in a similar political arrangement. The opposition leader made the claim at a news conference at the Peshawar high court on Friday.

Article Title: Pakistan to chair IMF, World Bank boards in 2027; first time in over 70 years
Article Text:
The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok (Photo: AP).

Pakistan will take over the chairmanship of the boards of governors of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in 2027, returning to the position for the first time since 1953, the country’s ministry of economic affairs said on Friday.The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, where Pakistan’s minister for economic affairs Ahad Khan Cheema, who also serves as the country’s governor to the World Bank, was formally designated as the incoming chair, PTI reported.Describing the appointment as a “historic milestone”, the ministry said the role would allow Pakistan to participate in shaping global economic and development discussions and encourage constructive engagement among member countries.The annual meetings, scheduled from October 12 to 18, have brought together more than 15,000 participants representing 191 countries.The appointment comes as Pakistan continues to rely on financial assistance from the IMF through two programmes: a USD 7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a USD 1.4 billion Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).While the EFF is aimed at meeting the country’s balance-of-payments needs and supporting economic reforms, the RSF provides longer-term funding to help Pakistan tackle climate-related risks and improve its resilience.Pakistan could receive a further USD 1.2 billion from the IMF, subject to approval by the fund’s Executive Board. The anticipated disbursement follows an agreement reached between IMF staff and Pakistani authorities on the latest reviews of both programmes.
Article Summary: Pakistan will take over the chairmanship of the boards of governors of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in 2027. The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok. Pakistan continues to rely on financial assistance from the IMF through two programmes.

Article Title: Pakistan ranks lowest in South Asia on hunger index amid rising food prices
Article Text:
Pakistan's 2026 Global Hunger Index standings reveal an alarming crisis, showcasing the worst performance in South Asia amid ongoing economic challenges. (Pic Credit: ANI)

Economic crisis and food inflation worsen Pakistan’s hunger situation

Hunger reduction stalls across South Asia

Extreme weather threatens regional food production

Millions across South Asia continue to face undernourishment

Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI), reflecting mounting food insecurity driven by economic instability, rising food prices, climate-related disasters and international conflicts, according to a report by Dawn.Titled “No Security Without Food Security”, the report was jointly prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas.According to the news agency ANI, the findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated, while Pakistan and Afghanistan have experienced a deterioration in conditions since 2018.Pakistan’s economic challenges and persistent food inflation have eroded household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for families to access sufficient and nutritious food.The report noted that Pakistan’s undernourishment indicator had deteriorated from a low level in 2018 to a medium level. Meanwhile, child wasting has approached the threshold associated with the high category, underscoring continuing concerns over child nutrition.South Asia recorded an overall global hunger index score of 23.5, placing the region in the serious category. While the score represents an improvement from 37.5 in 2000, the report suggests that much of the progress was achieved before 2018.Over the past two decades, Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved out of the alarming hunger category. However, persistent levels of child malnutrition continue to pose a significant challenge in both countries.Child stunting has continued to decline in Pakistan, while Afghanistan has recorded a slight increase in the indicator since 2018.Child mortality rates have improved in both countries, falling from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels in the latest assessment.The report also drew attention to the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural production and food security across South Asia.Heavy rainfall and flooding damaged crops in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh. In Afghanistan, inadequate rainfall and unusually high temperatures disrupted the cereal-growing season in 2026.These climate-related pressures could further aggravate food shortages and prolong acute food insecurity across the region, according to Dawn.Estimates from the food and agriculture organisation (FAO) indicate that approximately 218 million people across South Asia, including Iran, experienced undernourishment between 2023 and 2025.This represents roughly one-third of the global population affected by undernourishment during the period, highlighting the scale of the region’s food security challenge.The findings underscore the need for sustained efforts to address economic vulnerabilities, improve access to nutritious food and strengthen agricultural resilience against climate-related shocks.
Article Summary: Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI) The report was prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas. The findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated.

Article Title: 33 children, teacher killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan’s Peshawar
Article Text:
18 killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan's Peshawar

At least 33 students and a teacher were killed after the roof of a school collapsed in Pakistan 's Peshawar city on Thursday.Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident, officials said.Peshawar Capital City Police chief Mian Saeed said the incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area, as cited by PTI.Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Muhammad Asim said an emergency had been declared at the facility to treat the injured.All the children killed in the incident were aged 13 or younger, Asim said. Rescue officials said 25 injured children had been taken to medical facilities.Rescue teams were clearing the debris and searching for children and school staff who might still be trapped beneath the collapsed structure.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.Building and roof collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and the use of substandard construction materials.In July, three girls aged between three and 13 were killed when part of the outer wall of a government primary school near Umerkot collapsed, burying them under the debris, as cited by Dawn.That same month, a child was killed and at least five others were injured when the roof of an under-construction private school building collapsed in Lahore’s Baghbanpura neighbourhood.In June, 14 children died after the roof of a private tuition centre collapsed in Lahore’s Kahna area. Less than two months earlier, four children were killed and 20 people injured when a classroom roof collapsed at a private school in Dera Ghazi Khan.
Article Summary: Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident. The incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.

Article Title: Pakistan regulator warns TV channels against live coverage of blasts and terror attacks
Article Text:
The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight.

Channels told to air only verified information

Legal action for violations

Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks, cautioning that violations could lead to legal action.The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday, reminding broadcasters of restrictions first introduced on February 20, 2023. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting, rebroadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.The directive comes as emergency rule has been imposed in the north-western province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, renewing debate over how the media should report security incidents while ensuring that the public receives timely and reliable information.PEMRA has instructed broadcasters to air only “verified information warranted by the relevant government departments or law enforcement agencies”.The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight and the effective use of broadcast delays to prevent the immediate transmission of sensitive footage during security incidents.It directed television channels to establish independent editorial boards in line with applicable laws and relevant court judgments.The notification referred to the Supreme Court's judgment in Suo Motu Case No. 28 of 2018 and an Islamabad High Court order dated September 5, 2022, both concerning the prescribed procedure for broadcast delays.PEMRA warned that channels violating the directive could face legal proceedings under Sections 29A, 30 and 33 of the PEMRA Ordinance, 2002, as amended.The latest notification reiterates the regulator's existing restrictions on live coverage of security incidents, with a focus on verification, editorial checks and the use of broadcast delays.
Article Summary: Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.

Article Title: 6 killed, several injured as passenger train derails in Pakistan's Punjab
Article Text:
Train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan (Representative image) (PTI)

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to prevent train accidents? Improving railway tracks Upgrading safety systems Regular maintenance and inspections 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least six people were killed and several others injured after a passenger train derailed in Pakistan's Punjab province early Tuesday, Pakistan-based Geo News reported.The Rehman Baba Express, travelling from the southern port city of Karachi to the northwestern city of Peshawar, derailed in Sher Shah, Punjab province, news agency AP reported, citing Pakistan Railways spokesperson Kaleem Akhtar.The injured were taken to Nishtar Hospital in Multan for treatment, while rescue teams continued operations at the accident site.The accident took place at around 5.15am, according to Geo News.Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed grief over the deaths in separate statements and directed authorities to ensure the best possible medical care for the injured.Train accidents are relatively common in Pakistan, where the railway system has suffered from decades of underinvestment, outdated tracks and ageing signalling systems.In 2023, 10 carriages of a passenger train derailed in southern Pakistan, killing 30 people and injuring more than 90 others.
Article Summary: Passenger train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan. At least six people killed and several others injured in Sher Shah, Punjab province. Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif express grief over the deaths.

Article Title: 2 Pakistan army pilots killed as training aircraft crashes near Balochistan's Quetta
Article Text:
2 Pakistan army pilots killed (IANS photo)

Two Pakistan army pilots were killed after a Mushshak training aircraft crashed near Balochistan's Quetta on Monday due to a technical fault, as Dawn reported, citing the ISPR, the official media wing of the Pakistan armed forces.The Pakistan army identified the deceased as Major Husnain Shehzad Humayun, an instructor, and Captain Abdul Samad, a trainee pilot.The aircraft crashed near Nawan Killi in Quetta.In June, a Mi-17 helicopter belonging to the Pakistan army's aviation wing crashed during take-off near Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), reportedly due to a technical fault.All personnel on board were killed. The ISPR said rescue and recovery teams were rushed to the site and an inquiry was ordered to determine the cause of the crash, Dawn reported.In September last year, five crew members died when a Pakistan army helicopter crashed in the Diamer district of Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan (PoGB). The ISPR said the helicopter had encountered a technical fault.In August 2025, five crew members were also killed when a Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government helicopter carrying flood relief supplies crashed in a tribal district, Pakistan-based daily The Express Tribune reported.
Article Summary: Pakistan army identifies the deceased as Major Husnain Shehzad Humayun, an instructor, and Captain Abdul Samad, a trainee pilot. The aircraft crashed near Nawan Killi in Quetta. In June, a Mi-17 helicopter belonging to the Pakistan army's aviation wing crashed during take-off in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

Article Title: Bangladesh Hindu group condemns sealing of historic Ram Leela Temple in Pakistan
Article Text:
Pakistan seals centuries-old Hindu temple, commercial plaza plan triggers protests

Bangladesh Hindu Sammilon Sangho has expressed concern and strongly condemned the sealing of the centuries-old Ramlila Temple in Dera Ismail Khan, in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, amid reports of plans to demolish the historic structure and build a commercial complex on the site.In a statement issued on Saturday, the organisation said the reported move violated religious freedom and basic human rights. It also expressed solidarity with the local Hindu community and civil society members opposing the proposed construction."Our organisation, which firmly believes in the non-communal spirit of the great Liberation War, equality, and the core mantra of religious freedom, considers any attempt to destroy or force the closure of a place of worship to be a grave violation of basic human rights and freedom of religion", Bangladesh Hindu Sammilon Sangha said in a statement.According to media reports, the plan to demolish the historic temple and build a commercial building on its site was deeply tragic and contrary to global communal harmony."We extend our solidarity and full support to the brave resistance mounted by the local Hindu community and members of civil society against this attempt to destroy the historic structure", it added.The organisation urged the Pakistani government to protect the temple, stop any attempt to build a commercial complex at the site and restore the community’s right to conduct religious practices and rituals there.It also called for action against those responsible."We call upon the Government of Pakistan to immediately ensure the security of this historic and traditional temple, permanently halt all attempts to build a commercial complex, and restore the right to conduct religious practices and rituals at the location. At the same time, we demand exemplary punishment for those identified behind this heinous incident", the statement said."We also humbly request the international community to raise a stronger voice to protect minority rights and religious freedom in every corner of the world", it said.Earlier on Sunday, authorities in Dera Ismail Khan sealed the historic Ram Leela Temple in Rahim Bazaar, raising concerns over the protection of religious heritage and the proposed conversion of the site into a commercial property.The move came days after civil society activists intervened to prevent the building’s demolition for a commercial plaza, Dawn reported.According to the report, the temple had earlier been sealed by Assistant Commissioner Hamid Siddiq following public protests, and construction work at the site had been halted.The latest sealing has renewed concerns among residents and heritage advocates about the future of the historic structure. The development coincided with a joint meeting of civil society representatives and members of the Hindu community to discuss the reported demolition plans. Participants opposed the proposed commercial construction and urged elected representatives to raise the issue in Pakistan’s national assembly.
Article Summary: Bangladesh Hindu Sammilon Sangho condemns sealing of Ramlila Temple in Pakistan. Move comes amid reports of plans to demolish the historic structure and build a commercial complex on the site. The organisation said the reported move violated religious freedom and basic human rights.

Article Title: ‘I am not afraid’: Sheikh Hasina vows to return to Bangladesh in December
Article Text:
Speaking virtually at an event hosted by the Center for US-Bangladesh Relations in Washington, Hasina said it was her responsibility to return to Bangladesh.

Former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina on Monday reiterated her intention to return to Bangladesh in December, even if the Tarique Rahman-led government arrests, kills or tortures her.Speaking virtually at an event hosted by the Center for US-Bangladesh Relations in Washington, Hasina said it was her responsibility to return to Bangladesh.“I will go back to Bangladesh in December, I am not afraid. I know they can kill me, arrest me and torture me," Hasina said.“It’s my responsibility to go,” she added.
Article Summary: Former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina reiterated her intention to return to Bangladesh in December. Speaking virtually at an event hosted by the Center for US-Bangladesh Relations in Washington, Hasina said it was her responsibility to return. “It’s my responsibility to go,” she added.

Article Title: Graft charges at home, arrest in Qatar: Former Bangladesh Air Force chief held
Article Text:
Who is ACM (retd) Sheikh Abdul Hannan

(With PTI inputs)

Air chief marshal (retd) Sheikh Abdul Hannan of the Bangladesh Air Force was arrested in Qatar in connection with corruption charges against him in Bangladesh, an official in Dhaka said on Sunday.Akhtarul Islam, deputy director of Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), said Interpol had informed the anti-graft agency that Hannan was arrested by Qatari authorities on Thursday.“We have been informed by Interpol that Qatar’s law enforcement agency detained him there on October 15,” Islam told reporters in Dhaka.According to Islam, Hannan is accused of accumulating assets worth more than Tk 3.28 crore beyond his known sources of income and conducting suspicious transactions totalling Tk 27.63 crore through six personal bank accounts.Based on its findings, the ACC in July last year approved the filing of charges under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, Money Laundering Prevention Act and Prevention of Corruption Act.The former air chief's wife is also an accused in the case. She allegedly accumulated assets worth more than Tk 1.91 crore beyond her known sources of income, with her husband’s assistance.The ACC identified suspicious transactions totalling Tk 1.18 crore across 32 bank accounts held in her name.Investigators have traced Hannan’s alleged offshore wealth to Canada and Dubai and uncovered assets registered in the names of his children in three countries.In March, a Dhaka court ordered the seizure of income tax records belonging to Hannan and his wife following two separate applications by the ACC.According to the agency, Hannan managed to leave Bangladesh despite an active travel ban and several corruption cases against him.A court had also ordered the attachment of two apartments owned by the former air chief and the freezing of his bank accounts after the ACC accused him of accumulating wealth beyond his known sources of income.Hannan was commissioned into the Bangladesh Air Force in 1984 as a general duty (GD) pilot. He assumed office as the force’s 16th Chief of Air Staff on June 12, 2021, and retired on June 11, 2024.As per media reports, former Bangladesh Navy chief Admiral Mohammad Nazmul Hassan also faces corruption cases and is currently abroad, although no court has imposed a travel ban on him.Both Hannan and Hassan were appointed as service chiefs during the tenure of deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League government. Sheikh Hasina resigned as PM and left Bangladesh in August 2024 amid student-led public protests against her government.Hannan completed his tenure under the Awami League government, while Hassan retired during the subsequent interim administration led by Muhammad Yunus.
Article Summary: Air chief marshal (retd) Sheikh Abdul Hannan of the Bangladesh Air Force was arrested in Qatar in connection with corruption charges against him in Bangladesh. Hannan is accused of accumulating assets worth more than Tk 3.28 crore beyond his known sources of income.

Article Title: 'You are ruining entire town': With pistol in hand, Bangladesh minister raids drug den; watch
Article Text:
Bangladesh minister Ishraque Hossain raids a suspected drug den in Dhaka with a pistol in hand, sparking debate on social media

A Bangladeshi minister triggered a debate on social media after carrying out a raid on a suspected drug den in a Dhaka slum on Saturday, armed with a pistol and accompanied by associates, at least one of whom was also seen carrying a handgun.State minister for liberation war affairs Ishraque Hossain shared a video of the raid, showing him stepping out of a vehicle with a megaphone in one hand and a pistol in the other before chasing a group of people near Gandaria Railway Station.“You are ruining the entire town, destroying the entire area,” Hossain, 39, was heard telling the group in the footage, news agency PTI reported.Some of the men detained by his associates claimed they were innocent. “Let police come, then there will be talks,” Hossain was heard responding.Police said the minister had not informed them about the raid beforehand. He and his associates detained six people and handed them over to the local police station, according to officials."The minister did not inform us about the raid in advance; we learned about it afterwards,” Dhaka metropolitan police’s additional deputy commissioner Masud Rana told reporters.Hossain, a member of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), was elected to Parliament from the area in the February 12 elections.He posted the video on social media with the caption, “Ishraque's Action: Drug dens smashed and dealers handed over to the police.” The post also said he had previously conducted anti-drug raids in parts of his downtown Dhaka constituency and vowed to continue the campaign to make the area drug-free.Gendaria police station officer-in-charge Moniruzzaman Monir said officers went to the location after being informed that the men had been detained.“They detained six people and claimed they were drug abusers, so we went and brought them in,” he said.“Some powder was found in their possession, which will be tested to find out if the substance is a drug,” he added.
Article Summary: Ishraque Hossain shares video of raid on suspected drug den in Dhaka slum. Video shows him with megaphone in one hand, pistol in the other. He and associates detain six people and hand them over to local police station.

Article Title: Nepal PM, president stress unity and social harmony in Dashain messages
Article Text:
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah and President Ramchandra Paudel share heartfelt festive wishes for Bada Dashain, underlining family cohesion and social harmony. (Pic Credit: IANS)

PM remembers victims of devastating floods

President Paudel stresses harmony and cultural identity

Nepal Prime minister Balendra Shah and president Ramchandra Paudel on Saturday conveyed their greetings to the people on Bada Dashain, also known as Vijaya Dashami , the country's biggest festival, highlighting its importance in fostering family ties, social harmony and national unity.Their messages were issued on Phulpati, the seventh day of the 15-day Dashain festival. The occasion signals the start of the main festive period, when government offices close and celebrations gather momentum across Nepal.In his message, Prime Minister Shah said his government was committed to generating employment opportunities and promoting prosperity within the country so that Nepalis would not be compelled to travel abroad in search of work, according to the news agency PTI.Describing Bada Dashain as a festival that brings families together, Shah said it strengthens relationships, encourages unity and fosters closer bonds among people. He noted that the festival's religious, cultural and social significance had also helped connect Nepalis living across different parts of the world.“The sky itself feels different, the earth carries a unique fragrance, and the surroundings become naturally filled with joy and exuberance,” he said, describing the festive atmosphere.Shah observed that Nepalis had continued to celebrate Dashain and preserve their religious, cultural and social traditions despite numerous challenges over the years.Referring to the recent devastating flash floods in Bhotekoshi, Shah said this year's festivities had arrived while the country was still mourning the loss of lives and damage caused by the disaster. The floods left 1,455 people dead, 5,285 missing and more than 13,000 rescued, according to the figures cited in his message.The prime minister offered prayers for those who lost their lives, wished the injured a speedy recovery and expressed condolences to the affected families. He added that the government was working urgently to rehabilitate people displaced by the disaster.Shah also highlighted the traditional exchange of tika and jamara during Dashain. Tika, a mixture of vermilion powder, curd and rice, and jamara, consisting of barley shoots, are received from elders as symbols of respect for senior family members and affection for younger relatives.Nepalis traditionally receive tika and jamara from elders on Dashami, the festival's tenth day, which falls on October 21 this year.In a separate message, president Ramchandra Paudel extended his wishes for happiness, peace, prosperity, good health and continued progress to Nepalis living both within the country and abroad.Paudel said that while Nepal's diverse ethnic and religious communities follow their own customs and traditions, Bada Dashain plays a significant role in bringing families together and promoting social harmony, forgiveness, goodwill and fraternity.He added that the festival helps strengthen unity across Nepal's geographical, cultural and linguistic diversity while safeguarding the country's cultural identity.
Article Summary: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah and President Ramchandra Paudel send their greetings to the people on Bada Dashain. The messages were issued on Phulpati, the seventh day of the 15-day Dashain festival. The occasion signals the start of the main festive period.

Article Title: Afghanistan's lost five years under Taliban: Girls out of school, women out of work, millions hungry
Article Text:
Five years of Taliban rule in Afghanistan

Deepening crisis for Afghan women

Living with over 100 decrees: How Afghan women are walking on eggshells

The daily realities and escalating challenges facing Afghan women today​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​.

Shrinking lives of Afghan women

Class dismissed: Afghanistan’s girls locked out of learning

Education under Taliban

No freedom and a huge mental toll

A mental toll for Afghan women

Women out of work: A deepening crisis

Inflation and job losses deepen economic hardship

Women's exclusion comes at a steep economic cost

Food has gotten costlier over the years

Healthcare system left on ventilator

Number of teachers in Afghanistan over the years

Hunger games: Millions of Afghans have empty plate

Afghanistan's food crisis

Child malnutrition deepens the crisis

When the lifeline runs dry: Aid cuts leave Afghans in the lurc

Diminishing foreign aid for Afghanistan

Five years, countless restrictions: Afghanistan’s shrinking world

Parents report that their daughters are performing worse than expected (65%) compared to their sons (35%).

Five years of Taliban rule have left Afghanistan with so much loss and so little hope.Women have been pushed out of sight and eventually mind. Millions more face the threat of hunger as winter sets in.For a country that has already endured so much, hope is beginning to diminish.Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban has tightened its grip on everyday life, with women and girls bearing the brunt of its restrictions. Education, employment and freedom of movement have become increasingly difficult to access, while food insecurity, economic hardship, displacement and declining humanitarian assistance have deepened the crisis.“Today, the plight of many in Afghanistan is going from bad to worse,” UN Human Rights chief Volker Türk said, warning that the country's worsening situation was receiving inadequate international attention.“Yet, it seems the world has forgotten and abandoned the people of Afghanistan to a plight deepening by the day. The silence is deafening.”So, five years after the Taliban takeover, how has life changed for Afghans? Here are the numbers that tell the story.For women living under the Taliban’s rule, everyday chores such as going to work, visiting a market, studying or seeking medical care have become a Herculean task.According to UN Women, more than 100 decrees targeting women and girls have been issued since the Taliban returned to power.It began with education. Girls were barred from secondary education beyond Grade 6, followed by the exclusion of women from universities.Then by July 2023, beauty salons, among the remaining sources of income and female-only social spaces, were ordered to shut. Women were also barred from parks, gyms and public bathhouses.Almost a year later, Taliban formalised its Law on the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, imposing further controls on women's appearance and behaviour.Women were required to cover their bodies and faces in public and prohibited from raising their voices in public, including to sing or recite. Restrictions on employment, travel and dress, along with requirements to travel with a male guardian, further curtailed their freedom.And it's not just public life that the Taliban controls.In January 2026, the Taliban adopted a new Criminal Procedure Code for Courts that further highlighted the restrictions women face. Under Article 32, a husband who abuses his wife can face just 15 days in prison, and only if the abuse results in a broken bone, an open wound or a visible bruise.The code also allows husbands to impose discretionary punishments for “disobedience”, ranging from scolding to corporal punishment.Contrastingly, those who organise animal fights can face up to five months in prison.The restrictions have effectively shrunk women's everyday lives.According to a UN assessment, more than half of the women surveyed left home only once or twice a month. Nearly three-quarters felt unsafe leaving without a male guardian, while more than half avoided public spaces, including markets and healthcare facilities.Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are prohibited from accessing secondary and higher education under the current restrictions.According to UNICEF, more than 2.6 million girls had been denied secondary education since the Taliban takeover. Women had already been excluded from universities since December 2022, putting an end to an educational journey for millions.The consequences extend far beyond classrooms.Girls prevented from completing their education lose opportunities to pursue higher qualifications and skilled employment. Afghanistan, meanwhile, risks losing future teachers, doctors, nurses and other professionals needed to rebuild its institutions.The wider education system is also struggling. In January 2026, UNESCO and UNICEF reported that 93% of children completing primary school were still working towards basic reading proficiency.Between 2018 and 2024, the gross enrolment rate for boys fell from 120 to 104, while the rate for girls rose from 82 to 87. The overall rate declined from 101 to 95. Gross enrolment rates can exceed 100 because they include pupils outside the official age group and do not directly measure attendance or completion. The increase in girls' primary enrolment therefore does not mean restrictions on older girls have eased.The number of female teachers has also fallen, from 98,196 in 2019 to 66,208 in 2024, a decline of approximately 32.5%. UNICEF warned in April 2026 that Afghanistan could lose more than 25,000 female teachers and healthcare workers by 2030 if restrictions on girls' education and women's employment persist.The result could be a cycle of lost opportunity: girls are denied education today, fewer women qualify for professional jobs tomorrow, and future generations face a shrinking pool of trained educators and healthcare workers.The loss of education, employment and freedom of movement has taken a psychological toll on Afghan women.UN Women reported in August 2026 that 70% of women surveyed described their mental health as bad or very bad. An earlier UNDP assessment, based on consultations conducted in 2024, found that 81% of women consulted rated their mental health as bad or very bad. The figures come from different assessments and should not be interpreted as a direct trend.The UNDP review identified excessive worry, hopelessness or hypervigilance among the most frequently reported behavioural changes, affecting 37% of respondents. Excessive sadness was reported by 22%, decreased appetite or sleep by 21%, fatigue by 20% and social withdrawal by 12%.These pressures are closely linked to restrictions on women's everyday lives. A student unable to return to school may see her future narrowing before she can choose a career. A woman who loses her job may lose both income and independence, while someone who rarely leaves home may have fewer opportunities to maintain friendships or seek support.Accessing mental-health services can itself be difficult because of movement restrictions, limited services and financial pressures on community organisations.UNICEF's 2025 humanitarian reporting said it provided mental-health and psychosocial support to more than 2.2 million children and caregivers through community-based and media initiatives.Afghanistan's economic hardship has intensified as rising prices, job losses and cuts to international aid put further pressure on households.Inflation rose from an average of 3.6% in 2025 to 7.6% by March 2026, driven by higher food prices, supply disruptions and rising demand. Unemployment has almost doubled since 2021, according to the UN, while more than 500,000 jobs have disappeared.Women face additional barriers to earning a living. UN Women estimated that only 7% of Afghan women were employed, compared with 84% of men. Their continued exclusion could cost the country $920 million cumulatively between 2024 and 2026, equivalent to 5.8% of GDP.Financial insecurity is particularly severe in female-headed households. UNDP's 2025 socio-economic review found that unstable sources accounted for 65% of income in these households in 2024, compared with 43% in male-headed households.Some women have turned to small businesses, but restrictions on mobility, access to markets and finance make running them difficult. Lost jobs, rising prices and limits on women's earnings leave families with fewer ways to absorb economic shocks.The damage could persist for years. UNICEF estimated in April 2026 that restrictions on girls' education and women's employment were costing Afghanistan at least $84 million annually in lost economic output. This estimate and UN Women's cumulative projection cover different periods and use different methodologies, so they should not be combined.Restrictions on women's movement and a shortage of female medical professionals have made accessing treatment increasingly difficult.A February 2026 report by UN Special Rapporteur Richard Bennett found that movement restrictions, gender segregation and requirements to travel with a male guardian had severely limited women's access to healthcare. The absence of a male guardian could delay treatment even in emergencies.The shortage of female healthcare workers compounds the problem. Women were barred from medical and health education in December 2024, narrowing the pipeline of future doctors, nurses and midwives. In some regions, restrictions on women consulting male doctors make access to female medical professionals particularly important.Funding shortages have forced more than 440 health clinics to close or reduce services. The proportion of Afghans without access to healthcare rose from 16% in 2024 to 23% in 2025.Timely treatment is essential to prevent deaths from complications such as severe bleeding, high blood pressure, infections and obstructed labour. When women struggle to reach clinics or facilities that lack trained staff, the risks increase.Years of economic hardship, drought and declining international aid have left millions of Afghans struggling to afford basic necessities.An October 2026 assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme projected that 19.2 million people, or 38% of Afghanistan's population, would face acute food insecurity during November 2026-April 2027. This is up 10.3% from 17.4 million projected for the corresponding period a year earlier. Around five million people are expected to face emergency levels of hunger.Meanwhile, 21.9 million people, or about 45% of the population, are expected to need humanitarian assistance in 2026, including around 11.6 million children.Despite a relatively strong agricultural season, high food and transport costs, limited jobs, weak purchasing power, population movements and declining aid continue to undermine food access. Families may be forced to cut meals, buy less nutritious food or sacrifice other necessities, putting children and pregnant or breastfeeding women at particular risk.UNICEF reported in August 2026 that 3.7 million children were suffering from wasting, including around one million with severe acute malnutrition. Separately, supplied figures estimate that 3.5 million children under five are already experiencing acute malnutrition. These figures use different descriptions and require source checks before publication.Food-security assessments also projected that around four million women and children would need treatment for acute malnutrition in 2027, including approximately one million severe cases. These figures represent different measures and should not be added together.Funding shortages are already restricting access to help. The World Food Programme said in 2026 that it was turning away three out of four acutely malnourished children seeking assistance because it lacked funds to buy food.The United States, previously Afghanistan's largest donor, provided more than $3 billion in humanitarian and development assistance between October 2021 and December 2024. In January 2025, US President Donald Trump suspended US humanitarian funding for Afghanistan, removing a source that had accounted for about 45% of humanitarian support.The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan requires $1.71 billion to provide life-saving assistance and aims to reach 17.5 million people.As of August 2026, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs had recorded US$509.3 million, or 29.7% of the appeal, leaving a shortfall of approximately US$1.20 billion.Funding gaps have forced aid organisations to reduce coverage, interrupt supplies and close service points. Women and girls are particularly vulnerable when specialist services become unavailable.UN Women reported in August 2026 that nearly three-quarters of women-led organisations surveyed had experienced funding cuts in 2025, while more than half expected to suspend operations or close within the following year.The consequences extend across food assistance, nutrition and healthcare. With millions needing support, agencies face increasingly difficult choices about distributing scarce resources.Five years after the Taliban returned to power, Afghanistan is a country where everyday life has become a struggle for survival, dignity and hope. For women and girls, restrictions have turned once ordinary freedoms into distant possibilities.For millions of families, putting food on the table and accessing basic healthcare have become increasingly difficult. As economic hardship deepens and humanitarian support dwindles, the crisis is reaching into every corner of Afghan life.But what has changed since the Taliban takeover, and what does it mean for the country's future?The numbers paint a grim picture.
Article Summary: Five years of Taliban rule have left Afghanistan with so much loss and so little hope. Education, employment and freedom of movement have become increasingly difficult to access. Food insecurity, economic hardship, displacement and declining humanitarian assistance have deepened the crisis.
